questions.stem: Consider the following two finite automata $D_1$ and $D_2$. Which of the following statements is/are true?
questions.figure: D1 has six states; the start state S is the only accepting state. Transitions of D1: S on 0 to A; S on 1 to D; A on 0 to B; A on 1 to C; B on 0 to S; B on 1 to S; C on 0 to S; D on 0 to E; E on 1 to S. D2 has five states; the start state S is the only accepting state. Transitions of D2: S on 0 to P; S on 1 to R; P on 1 to Q; Q on 1 to S; R on 0 to T; R on 1 to Q; R on 1 to T; T on 0 to S. State R has two arrows on 1, so D2 is nondeterministic. A missing arrow means the string dies. The drawing has no state names; S, A to E and P to T are ours.

diagram.alt: Two automata side by side. D1 has six states with the start state accepting, and loops of length three back to it. D2 has five states with the start state accepting, and its state R has two arrows labelled 1.

solutionDiagram.alt: D1 and D2 with named states. Every route from the start state S back to S reads exactly three symbols: D1 gives 000, 001, 010, 101 and D2 gives 011, 111, 100, 110.

options: $(L(D_1) \cup L(D_2))^*$ consists of all strings in $\{0,1\}^*$ whose length is divisible by 3

steps.title: What the automaton accepts, and the one rule used here
steps.body: A finite automaton reads a string one symbol at a time and, at each step, follows an arrow labelled with that symbol. A double circle marks an accepting state. The automaton accepts the string if, after the last symbol, it can be in an accepting state; $L(D)$ is the set of all accepted strings. If no arrow with the needed label exists, that attempt dies and the string is rejected on that path. An automaton like $D_2$, where one state has two arrows with the same label, is nondeterministic: it accepts if at least one path works. In both pictures the start state S is the only accepting state, so a string is accepted exactly when the machine is back in S after the last symbol. That gives the rule: $L(D)$ is every concatenation of loops that leave S and return to S, and the empty string $\epsilon$ is accepted because S is both start and accepting.

steps.title: List the loops of D1
steps.body: Follow every route that leaves S and returns to S for the first time. S reads 0 to A. From A, reading 0 reaches B, and from B either symbol returns to S: this gives $000$ and $001$. From A, reading 1 reaches C, and C on 0 returns to S: this gives $010$. S reads 1 to D, D reads 0 to E, E reads 1 to S: this gives $101$. Every loop has length 3, so

steps.title: List the loops of D2
steps.body: S reads 0 to P, P reads 1 to Q, Q reads 1 to S: $011$. S reads 1 to R. From R, reading 1 can go to Q and then Q on 1 returns to S: $111$. From R, reading 0 goes to T and T on 0 returns to S: $100$. From R, reading 1 can also go to T, and T on 0 returns to S: $110$. Again every loop has length 3, so

steps.title: Compare the two block sets
steps.body: There are exactly eight binary strings of length 3. $D_1$ takes $\{000,001,010,101\}$ and $D_2$ takes the other four, $\{011,100,110,111\}$, so the two block sets are disjoint and together cover all eight. (A) is false: $000\in L(D_1)$ but $000\notin L(D_2)$. (B) is false for the same reason, since $L(D_1)$ is not even contained in $L(D_2)$.

steps.title: Judge (C) and (D)
steps.body: (C): a non-empty string in both languages has a length that is a multiple of 3 and splits into blocks of 3 symbols at fixed positions, so its first block would lie in both block sets, which are disjoint. Hence the only common string is $\epsilon$, and (C) is true. (D): any string whose length is divisible by 3 splits into blocks of 3, each block is one of the eight strings, and each of the eight lies in one of the two block sets, so the string is in $(L(D_1)\cup L(D_2))^*$. Conversely every string in that star has length divisible by 3. So (D) is true. The answer is (C) and (D).

shortcut.body: Write the length-3 loops of each machine (4 strings each) and notice they are complementary halves of the 8 strings of length 3. Then (C) and (D) follow in one line, and (A), (B) fail on the string $000$. This takes about 2 minutes. It is safe here because every loop has the same length; if the loops had different lengths, a string could split in two ways and (C) would need a closer check.

traps.text: Choosing (A) because both pictures look alike: each machine returns to S after blocks of length 3. They accept different blocks, so the languages differ, for example on $000$.
Choosing (B) after noticing that $D_2$ has more arrows. The number of arrows says nothing about containment: $000\in L(D_1)$ is not in $L(D_2)$.

Leaving out (C) because it looks like the intersection should be the empty set. The start state is accepting in both machines, so $\epsilon$ is in both languages and the intersection is $\{\epsilon\}$, not $\emptyset$.
Leaving out (D) after checking only one machine. The union has all eight blocks, and every string of length divisible by 3 is built from them, so the star covers all such strings.

recognize.clues: Both drawn machines have the start state as their only accepting state, so each language is a chain of loops through S. State R in $D_2$ has two arrows on 1, which marks $D_2$ as nondeterministic.
recognize.contrast: This is not a closure-property question about arbitrary regular languages. The loops are concrete strings, so list them and compare the two sets; closure only tells you the star of a union is regular.

check.body: Run concrete strings through both machines. The string $000111$ splits into the blocks $000$ and $111$, so $000\in L(D_1)$ and $111\in L(D_2)$ put it in $(L(D_1)\cup L(D_2))^*$, yet neither machine alone accepts it, since its first block lies in only one block set. The string $100$ is accepted by $D_2$ and rejected by $D_1$, so the languages differ. Finally $0000$ has length 4, not a multiple of 3, and is in neither language.

questions.stem: Let M be a nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) with 6 states over a finite alphabet. Which of the following options CANNOT be the number of states in the minimal deterministic finite automaton (DFA) that is equivalent to $M$ ?

solutionDiagram.alt: Six-state NFA in a row: q0 loops on 0 and 1, q0 moves to q1 on 1, then q1 to q5 on either symbol; q5 accepts. It accepts strings whose 5th symbol from the right is 1 and its minimal DFA has 32 states.

steps.title: What NFA, DFA and the subset construction are
steps.body: An NFA may be in several states at once after reading a prefix; a DFA is in exactly one state. To turn an NFA into a DFA, the subset construction makes each DFA state stand for a set of NFA states, namely the set the NFA could be in. An NFA with $n$ states has only $2^n$ different subsets, so the resulting DFA has at most $2^n$ states, counting the empty set (which acts as the dead state). The minimal DFA for the same language is never larger than that one. The rule for the question: the minimal DFA of a 6-state NFA has at most $2^6$ states, and any number between 1 and that bound is possible provided an example exists.

steps.title: Apply the upper bound
steps.body: With $n=6$ the ceiling is $2^6=64$. The options 65 and 128 are both larger than 64, so no 6-state NFA can have a minimal DFA with that many states. These are options (B) and (D).

steps.title: Show that 1 and 32 can happen
steps.body: One state: let all six states of $M$ be accepting and let every state loop on every symbol. Then $L(M)=\Sigma^*$ and the minimal DFA is a single accepting state. 32 states: take the language 'the 5th symbol from the right is 1'. An NFA with 6 states $q_0,\dots,q_5$ guesses the position: $q_0$ loops on every symbol, $q_0\to q_1$ on 1, and $q_1\to q_2\to q_3\to q_4\to q_5$ on any symbol, with $q_5$ accepting. A DFA must remember the last 5 symbols. Two different 5-bit strings $u,v$ differ at some position $i$ counted from the left; appending $0^{i-1}$ makes that position the 5th from the right, so one is accepted and the other not. All $2^5=32$ strings are therefore pairwise distinguishable, and a DFA that keeps the last 5 symbols has exactly 32 states. A script that runs the subset construction and minimizes confirms 32. So (A) and (C) are possible, and the answer is (B) and (D).
steps.tex: u z \in L,\ v z\notin L\quad\text{for } z=0^{\,i-1}

shortcut.body: Compute $2^6=64$ and cross out every option above 64: 65 and 128. The other two, 1 and 32, are clearly reachable (the universal language, and the '5th symbol from the right' language). About 30 seconds. The shortcut checks only the ceiling; it is safe because an arbitrary alphabet is allowed, so every size from 1 to 64 can be built.

traps.text: Rejecting 32 because it is not 64. The bound is a maximum, not the only value: the 'fifth from the right is 1' language reaches exactly 32.
Rejecting 1 on the belief that a 6-state NFA needs at least 6 DFA states. Extra NFA states can be redundant: a 6-state NFA for $\Sigma^*$ has a one-state minimal DFA.
Accepting 65 as $2^6+1$, where the extra state is a dead state. The empty set is already one of the 64 subsets, so the dead state is counted inside 64.
Accepting 128 by using $2^{n+1}$ or $2^7$, perhaps by adding a start state. The bound for an $n$-state NFA is $2^n$, with no extra factor.

recognize.clues: The wording pairs 'an NFA with 6 states' with 'the number of states in the minimal DFA' and asks which numbers CANNOT occur. That is the $2^n$ blow-up bound of the subset construction, read as a range of possible sizes.
recognize.contrast: Minimization merges equivalent states of a DFA you are given. No DFA is given here, so the question is about the range of sizes that converting an NFA can produce, not about merging table entries.

check.body: Run the bound on a case small enough to list. The language 'the 2nd symbol from the right is 1' has a 3-state NFA ($q_0$ loops on both symbols, $q_0\to q_1$ on 1, $q_1\to q_2$ on either symbol, $q_2$ accepting). The prefixes $00,01,10,11$ are pairwise separated by the suffixes $0$ and $1$, so its minimal DFA has exactly 4 states, and the 3-state ceiling is $2^3=8$, which is not exceeded. The same family with 6 NFA states gives $2^5=32$, and the cap is $2^6=64$, so 65 and 128 are impossible.

questions.stem: Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be two languages over a finite alphabet, such that $L_1 \cap L_2$ and $L_2$ are regular languages. Which of the following statements is/are always true?

steps.title: Definitions and what 'always true' demands
steps.body: A language is regular if some finite automaton accepts it, and context-free if some context-free grammar generates it; every regular language is context-free. The complement $\overline{L}$ is the set of strings over the alphabet that are not in $L$. Regular languages are closed under complement, union and intersection, meaning that applying those operations to regular languages gives a regular language. A statement is 'always true' only if it holds for every pair $L_1,L_2$ that meets the hypothesis, so a single pair that breaks it makes the statement false. The hypothesis restricts only $L_2$ and the part of $L_1$ that lies inside $L_2$.

steps.title: One counterexample kills (A), (B) and (D)
steps.body: Take $L_2=\emptyset$, which is regular. For any $L_1$ we get $L_1\cap L_2=\emptyset$, also regular, so the hypothesis holds whatever $L_1$ is. Choose $L_1=\{a^nb^nc^n\mid n\ge 0\}$, which is not context-free and therefore not regular. Then (A) '$L_1$ is regular' is false, and (D) '$L_1$ is context-free' is false. For (B), $L_1\cup L_2=L_1\cup\emptyset=L_1$, which is not regular, so (B) is false.
steps.tex: L_2=\emptyset,\quad L_1=\{a^nb^nc^n\}:\qquad L_1\cap L_2=\emptyset,\quad L_1\cup L_2=L_1

steps.title: Why (C) always holds
steps.body: $L_2$ is regular, regular languages are closed under complement, so $\overline{L_2}$ is regular. Every regular language is context-free, so $\overline{L_2}$ is context-free. This uses only the hypothesis on $L_2$, so it holds in every case. The answer is (C).

shortcut.body: Substitute $L_2=\emptyset$ (regular, and $L_1\cap\emptyset=\emptyset$ for any $L_1$) and pick a wild $L_1$ such as $\{a^nb^nc^n\}$: that disposes of (A), (B) and (D) at once. Then (C) is the closure of regular languages under complement plus regular implies context-free. About one minute. Always test the extreme case $L_2=\emptyset$ or $L_2=\Sigma^*$ first.

traps.text: Reading '$L_1\cap L_2$ and $L_2$ regular' as 'cancel $L_2$ and conclude $L_1$ is regular'. The intersection sees only the part of $L_1$ inside $L_2$; the part of $L_1$ outside $L_2$ is unconstrained.
Thinking the union is regular because both pieces mentioned are regular. $L_1\cup L_2$ still contains all of $L_1$, including the part outside $L_2$, so it can be non-regular.
Rejecting (C) because the hypothesis names $L_2$, not its complement. Regular languages are closed under complement, so $\overline{L_2}$ is regular, hence context-free.
Assuming $L_1$ must be at least context-free because it meets a regular set. With $L_2=\emptyset$ the hypothesis holds for any $L_1$, even a language that is not context-free.

recognize.clues: The phrase 'always true' with assumptions about $L_1\cap L_2$ and $L_2$ only means you may use closure rules on the regular parts and must test every claim about $L_1$ with a counterexample.
recognize.contrast: Do not read regularity of $L_1\cap L_2$ as regularity of $L_1$. Closure says regular inputs give regular outputs; it does not run backwards from an output to its inputs.

check.body: The complement claim needs nothing about $L_1$: take a DFA for $L_2$ and swap its accepting and non-accepting states to get a DFA for $\overline{L_2}$. As a boundary test, $L_2=\emptyset$ gives $\overline{L_2}=\Sigma^*$ and $L_2=\Sigma^*$ gives $\overline{L_2}=\emptyset$, both regular and so both context-free.

questions.stem: Let $\Sigma = \{a, b, c\}$. For $x \in \Sigma^*$, and $\alpha \in \Sigma$, let $\#_\alpha(x)$ denote the number of occurrences of $\alpha$ in $x$. Which one or more of the following option(s) define(s) regular language(s)?

solutionDiagram.alt: A grid of 7 columns (a count modulo 7) by 9 rows (b count modulo 9): 63 cells, reading a moves one column right, reading b moves one row down, start at column 0 row 0, accepting cell at column 2 row 3.

steps.title: What makes a language regular
steps.body: A language is regular when a finite automaton accepts it. A finite automaton has finitely many states, which is finite memory: it can remember a bounded amount of the past, for example a count modulo a fixed number $k$ (the remainder after dividing by $k$), but it cannot remember an unbounded count. Test: if infinitely many prefixes $u_1,u_2,\dots$ each need a different suffix to finish correctly, a finite automaton would need infinitely many states, so the language is not regular (Myhill-Nerode). The rule for this question: remainders modulo fixed constants are regular, and comparing two unbounded counts is not.

steps.title: Option (A): regular
steps.body: $a^mb^n$ with $m,n\ge0$ is the expression $a^*b^*$: read a's, then b's, with no relation between $m$ and $n$. A 3-state DFA (a-state, b-state, dead state) accepts it. Regular.

steps.title: Option (B): not regular
steps.body: A string of the second set has $m-n$ copies of $c$ at the end. For it to also lie in $\{a,b\}^*$ it must contain no $c$, so $m-n=0$. The intersection is therefore $\{a^nb^n\mid n\ge0\}$. For $i\ne j$ the prefixes $a^i$ and $a^j$ are told apart by the suffix $b^i$: $a^ib^i$ is in the set and $a^jb^i$ is not. That gives infinitely many classes, so it is not regular. Intersecting with the regular set $\{a,b\}^*$ does not rescue it: a regular set intersected with a non-regular one can be regular or not, and here the result is $\{a^nb^n\}$.

steps.title: Option (C): regular
steps.body: Keep two counters at the same time: $\#_a \bmod 7$ and $\#_b \bmod 9$. Reading $a$ adds 1 to the first counter, reading $b$ adds 1 to the second. A state is the pair $(x,y)$ with $x\in\{0,\dots,6\}$ and $y\in\{0,\dots,8\}$: $7\cdot9=63$ states, start $(0,0)$, accepting $(2,3)$. A script confirms that the minimal DFA has exactly 63 states. Regular.

steps.title: Option (D): not regular
steps.body: Take the prefixes $a^2,a^9,a^{16},\dots$, that is $a^i$ with $i\equiv2\pmod7$. The string $a^ib^i$ is in the language (equal counts, $\#_a=i\equiv2$), while $a^jb^i$ with $j\ne i$ is not. So these prefixes are pairwise distinguishable and there are infinitely many classes: not regular. The modulo-7 clause does not help, because the equality of the two unbounded counts is still required. The answer is (A) and (C).
steps.tex: a^ib^i\in L\iff i\equiv 2\pmod 7,\qquad a^jb^i\notin L\ (j\ne i)

shortcut.body: Scan each option for the type of condition. Remainders modulo fixed numbers, or a fixed order like $a^*b^*$, give finite memory: regular, so (A) and (C). A relation between two unbounded counts ($m=n$ in (B) after the $c$'s vanish, or $\#_a=\#_b$ in (D)) gives infinite memory: not regular. About 2 minutes. The scan is safe here, but an equality of counts can be regular in other settings (for example '#01 equals #10'), so confirm with a distinguishing suffix when in doubt.

traps.text: Seeing '$\{a,b\}^*\cap$ something' and concluding regular because $\{a,b\}^*$ is regular. A regular set intersected with a non-regular set can come out either way, so compute the intersection instead of arguing from the closure rule. Here $\{a^mb^nc^{m-n}\}$ is not regular and the intersection collapses to $\{a^nb^n\}$, which is not regular either.
Choosing (D) because the clause $\#_a\equiv2\pmod 7$ looks like a counter. The second clause $\#_a=\#_b$ compares two unbounded counts, which forces infinitely many states.
Leaving out (A) because $a^mb^n$ resembles $a^nb^n$. In (A) the exponents $m$ and $n$ are independent, so the language is just $a^*b^*$.
Leaving out (C) because two moduli look like too much counting. Both counters are bounded (7 and 9 values), so a product DFA of 63 states suffices.

recognize.clues: Each option is a condition on counts or order in $\{a,b\}^*$: remainders modulo constants, a fixed order $a^mb^n$, and equalities between counts. Those conditions decide whether finite memory suffices.
recognize.contrast: A remainder modulo a constant needs finite memory, while equality of two unbounded counts needs infinite memory. Adding a modulo clause to an equality clause does not make the language regular.

check.body: Second route for an equal-count option: take $a^{p}b^{p}$ with $p$ at least the pumping length and $p\equiv2\pmod 7$. The pumped part lies inside the $a$'s, so pumping up changes $\#_a$ but not $\#_b$ and breaks the equality. For the pair-of-remainders option, $a^2b^3$ and $a^9b^{12}$ must get the same verdict, since only remainders count.

questions.stem: Let $\Sigma = \{1,2,3,4\}$. For $x \in \Sigma^*$, let $prod(x)$ be the product of symbols in $x$ modulo 7. We take $prod(\epsilon) = 1$, where $\epsilon$ is the null string. For example, $prod(124) = (1 \times 2 \times 4) \bmod 7 = 1$. Define $L = \{x \in \Sigma^* \mid prod(x) = 2\}$. The number of states in a minimum state DFA for $L$ is __________. (Answer in integer)

solutionDiagram.alt: Six states labelled by the residues 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5 arranged on a hexagon; reading symbol 3 moves one step around it. State 1 is the start and state 2 is accepting.

steps.title: What 'minimum state DFA' counts
steps.body: Two strings $u$ and $v$ are equivalent for $L$ when no suffix $z$ can tell them apart, that is, for every $z$ the strings $uz$ and $vz$ are either both in $L$ or both outside it. The minimum DFA has exactly one state for each equivalence class (Myhill-Nerode), so the question asks for the number of classes. Here $prod(x)$ is the product of the symbols modulo 7, the remainder when the product is divided by 7. The rule: the future of a string depends only on $prod(x)$, and two residues are different classes exactly when some suffix sends one to 2 and the other elsewhere.

steps.title: Residues are enough, and which residues occur
steps.body: Appending a symbol $s$ multiplies the residue: $prod(xs)=(prod(x)\cdot s)\bmod 7$. So a DFA whose states are residues, start 1, move $r\xrightarrow{s}(rs)\bmod 7$, accepting 2, recognizes $L$. The residue 0 never occurs, because 7 is prime and no symbol is a multiple of 7. Symbol 3 alone walks through every nonzero residue: $1\to3\to2\to6\to4\to5\to1$ (since $3\cdot3=9\equiv2$, $2\cdot3=6$, $6\cdot3=18\equiv4$, $4\cdot3=12\equiv5$, $5\cdot3=15\equiv1$). All six residues $1,\dots,6$ are reachable.

steps.title: Show the six residues are pairwise distinguishable
steps.body:
Take residues $r
e s$. Because 7 is prime, $r$ has an inverse modulo 7, so there is a target $t=2r^{-1} mod 7$ with $rt\equiv2$. Every target is the product of some word over $\{1,2,3,4\}$: $t=1,2,3,4$ by the single symbols, $t=6$ by $23$, $t=5$ by $43$. The suffix $z$ for target $t$ sends $r$ to 2 (accepted) and sends $s$ to $2sr^{-1}
e2$ (rejected), because $s
e r$. So no two states can be merged. For example, residue 1 needs $z=2$, residue 3 needs $z=3$, residue 5 needs $z=23$ and residue 6 needs $z=43$; a script that minimizes the 6-state DFA confirms there is no merge. The minimum DFA has 6 states.

shortcut.body: The state is the running product mod 7, which can be any of the 6 nonzero residues, and 3 generates all of them, so all 6 are reachable. With a prime modulus every nonzero residue is invertible, so none merge: answer 6. About 1.5 minutes. Unsafe if the modulus were composite (for example mod 6 or 8): zero divisors make some residues collapse, and you would have to compute the classes.

traps.text: 7: counting the residue 0 as a state. A product of symbols from $\{1,2,3,4\}$ is never a multiple of 7, so 0 is unreachable and does not belong to the DFA.
2 or 3: thinking only 'is the product 2 or not' matters. The next symbol changes the residue, so the DFA must remember which residue it is in, not only whether it equals 2.
4 or 5: merging residues that look symmetric, such as 3 and 4. They need different suffixes to reach 2 (3 needs $z=3$, 4 needs $z=4$), so they stay apart.
7 again by adding a dead state: the DFA is already complete, since every symbol is defined on every residue, so no dead state exists.

recognize.clues: 'Minimum state DFA' for a product taken modulo a prime: each class of strings is a residue, and the symbols decide which residues are reachable and whether they can be separated.
recognize.contrast: Minimization topic merges states of a DFA that is already drawn. Here no table is given, so you build the classes yourself by proving reachability and distinguishability.

check.body: Spot-check two pairs of residues. Strings $2$ and $4$ have residues 2 and 4, and the empty suffix already separates them since only $2$ is in $L$. Strings $1$ and $3$ are separated by the suffix $2$, which gives residues 2 and 6. Residue 0 never appears, so there is no dead state to add to the count.

questions.stem: A regular language $L$ is accepted by a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with $n$ states. Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE?
options: $L$ may have an accepting NFA with $< n$ states.
$L$ may have an accepting DFA with $< n$ states.
There exists a DFA with $\le 2^n$ states that accepts $L$.
Every DFA that accepts $L$ has $> 2^n$ states.

steps.title: The terms and the facts that decide each option
steps.body: An NFA may have several arrows with the same label from a state; a DFA has exactly one. Both accept exactly the regular languages. The subset construction converts an $n$-state NFA into a DFA whose states are sets of NFA states, so that DFA has at most $2^n$ states. Words matter: 'may have' is true if one language and one NFA make it true; 'there exists' is a claim about every $L$; 'every DFA that accepts $L$' says the property holds for all DFAs for $L$, so one small DFA refutes it. We are asked for the FALSE statements.

steps.title: Statements (A) and (B)
steps.body: Let $L=\Sigma^*$ and give it an $n$-state NFA that wastes states (all states accepting, every state looping on every symbol). Then $L$ also has a 1-state NFA and a 1-state DFA, both with fewer than $n$ states when $n\ge2$. So (A) and (B) are true: they say it may happen, and it does.

steps.title: Statement (C)
steps.body: By the subset construction, every language accepted by an $n$-state NFA is accepted by a DFA with at most $2^n$ states. This is a theorem, not just an example, so (C) is true for every $L$. A script that runs the construction on the NFA for 'the 4th symbol from the right is 1' (5 states) gets a minimal DFA of 16 states, below the bound $2^5=32$.

steps.title: Statement (D) is the false one
steps.body: (D) claims that every DFA for $L$ has more than $2^n$ states. By (C) there is a DFA with at most $2^n$ states, so (D) is false for every regular $L$; the language $\Sigma^*$ gives an even starker case, a DFA with 1 state. The only false statement is (D).
steps.tex: \exists\ \text{DFA with}\le 2^n\ \text{states}\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{'every DFA has}>2^n\text{ states' is false}

shortcut.body: Match each option to the subset-construction theorem: (C) is the theorem, so true. (D) is its direct negation, so false. (A) and (B) say 'may', and the universal language with a padded NFA satisfies both. About 1 minute. Unsafe if you read 'may' as 'must'; then (A) and (B) look false.

traps.text: Marking (A) false because an $n$-state NFA 'needs' $n$ states. The word is 'may': redundant states or an easy language give a smaller NFA.
Marking (B) false by assuming a DFA can never be smaller than the NFA. A DFA is often larger, but for easy languages such as $\Sigma^*$ it can be smaller.

Marking (C) false after confusing the bound $2^n$ with $2n$ or by thinking some NFAs need more. The subset construction caps every case at $2^n$; the cap is a worst case that most NFAs stay well under.

Leaving (D) unmarked because 'more than $2^n$ states' sounds like the worst case of the subset construction. The construction gives an upper bound of $2^n$, so a DFA with more than $2^n$ states is never forced, and 'every DFA' is false.

recognize.clues: The question mixes the state count $n$ of an NFA with DFA state counts, and uses the words 'may', 'there exists' and 'every'. That is the $2^n$ bound of the subset construction plus quantifier reading.
recognize.contrast: The $2^n$ bound is a ceiling for the smallest DFA, not a floor, so a DFA can be far below it. It also says nothing that forces every DFA to be large.

check.body: Test the smallest case. A 1-state NFA that accepts every string has $2^1=2$ as its bound, and a single DFA state already accepts the same language. So a statement demanding every DFA to have more than $2^n$ states fails even here, which agrees with (D) being false.

questions.stem: Consider the following two languages over the alphabet $\{a, b\}$: $L_1 = \{ \alpha\beta\alpha \mid \alpha \in \{a, b\}^+ \text{ AND } \beta \in \{a, b\}^+ \}$ and $L_2 = \{ \alpha\beta\alpha \mid \alpha \in \{a\}^+ \text{ AND } \beta \in \{a, b\}^+ \}$. Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT?

solutionDiagram.alt: Five-state minimal DFA for L2, the strings that start with a, end with a and have length at least 3: q0 start, q1 after a, q2 for strings that start with a, have length at least 2 and are not accepted yet, q3 accepting, plus a dead state for strings starting with b.

options: $L_1$ is a regular language but $L_2$ is not a regular language.
$L_1$ is not a regular language but $L_2$ is a regular language.
Neither $L_1$ nor $L_2$ is a regular language.

steps.title: What the notation says and how regularity is tested
steps.body: A string $w$ is in $L_1$ if it can be cut as $\alpha\,\beta\,\alpha$: some non-empty $\alpha$ is both a prefix and a suffix, with a non-empty $\beta$ left between the two copies, so $|w|\ge2|\alpha|+1$. The superscript $+$ means one or more symbols. $L_2$ is the same but $\alpha$ may use only the letter $a$. A language is regular if a finite automaton accepts it. The Myhill-Nerode test: if infinitely many strings pairwise need different suffixes to complete, a finite automaton would need infinitely many states, so the language is not regular. The rule: a decision about $L$ must be made on all valid $\alpha$, not only the shortest ones.

steps.title: L2 is regular
steps.body: If $w=\alpha\beta\alpha$ with $\alpha=a^k$, then $w$ starts with $a$, ends with $a$, and has length at least 3. Conversely, if $w$ starts with $a$, ends with $a$, and has length at least 3, take $\alpha=a$ and $\beta$ the middle part (non-empty). So $L_2$ is exactly the set of strings that start with $a$, end with $a$ and have length at least 3, which is the regular expression $a(a+b)^+a$. A 5-state DFA accepts it, and it is minimal (see the drawing): the states are start, 'just a', 'started with a but not yet accepting', accepting, and dead. A script over all strings up to length 12 confirms the match.

steps.title: L1 contains strings whose first and last symbols differ
steps.body: If we only tried the one-letter $\alpha$, we would find 'first symbol equals last symbol, length at least 3' and call $L_1$ regular. But $\alpha$ can be longer: $abaab=ab\cdot a\cdot ab$ is in $L_1$ although it starts with $a$ and ends with $b$. So the structure of $L_1$ is richer. Look at strings of the form $a\,b^i\,a\,b^j$ with $i,j\ge0$.

steps.title: A family that forces unbounded memory
steps.body: Claim: $ab^iab^j\in L_1$ exactly when $i>j$. If $j=0$ the string starts and ends with $a$, and has length $i+2\ge3$ when $i\ge1$, so it is in $L_1$ when $i>0$. If $j\ge1$ the first symbol is $a$ and the last is $b$, so $\alpha$ must begin with $a$ and end with $b$, and as a suffix of the string it must be $ab^j$ (the part after the last $a$ onward). It also has to appear as a prefix, so $ab^j$ must be a prefix of $ab^iab^j$, which needs $j\le i$, and it must leave a non-empty $\beta$: $i+j+2\ge2(j+1)+1$, which is $i\ge j+1$. A longer $\alpha$ would have to contain the second $a$ and then be longer than half of the string. A script that tests all $i,j<10$ confirms the claim.

steps.title: Apply Myhill-Nerode to L1
steps.body: Take the prefixes $ab^1a,\ ab^2a,\ ab^3a,\dots$ For $i<i'$ use the suffix $z=b^i$: $ab^{i'}a\,b^i$ has $i'>i$, so it is in $L_1$, while $ab^iab^i$ has $i=i$, so it is not. Hence all these prefixes are pairwise distinguishable, giving infinitely many classes, and $L_1$ is not regular. $L_2$ is regular. This is option (C).

shortcut.body: For $L_2$ the border is made of $a$'s only, so it collapses to 'start with $a$, end with $a$, length at least 3': regular. That removes (B) and (D). For $L_1$, the border $\alpha$ is any string over two letters and can be arbitrarily long; the machine would have to store it to compare with the end, as for $ww$-type languages: not regular, so (C). About 3 minutes. This is a pattern judgment, not a proof; the proof is the family $ab^iab^j$.

traps.text: Choosing (A) after noticing that $\alpha=$ a single letter gives 'first symbol equals last symbol', a regular condition. The definition allows any non-empty $\alpha$, and longer borders such as $ab$ put strings like $abaab$ into $L_1$.
Swapping the roles: thinking the restriction $\alpha\in\{a\}^+$ makes $L_2$ harder. With only $a$'s the border collapses to one letter, which makes $L_2$ easier, not harder.

Choosing (D) on the idea that every language of the shape $\alpha\beta\alpha$ is like $ww$ and is not regular. In $L_2$ the border can always be shortened to the single letter $a$, so no memory is needed.

recognize.clues: Each string is cut as $\alpha\beta\alpha$, a border repeated at both ends. The two languages differ only in what $\alpha$ may be, a string over two letters or a run of $a$'s, and that decides how much must be stored.
recognize.contrast: The pumping lemma can also prove non-regularity, but it needs a string chosen against an arbitrary pumping length. The prefix-separating argument fits the border pattern more directly.

check.body: Test strings. $abaab$ equals $ab\cdot a\cdot ab$, so it is in $L_1$ although its first and last symbols differ, while in $L_2$ the block must be all $a$'s, so it is out. $aba$ is in both languages with $\alpha=a$ and $\beta=b$. $aa$ is in neither, since $\beta$ must be non-empty.

questions.stem: Consider the following deterministic finite automaton (DFA) defined over the alphabet, $\Sigma = \{a, b\}$. Identify which of the following language(s) is/are accepted by the given DFA.
questions.figure: Four states in a row, left to right: q0 (start), q1, q2, q3 (accepting, double circle). Transitions: q0 on a loops to q0; q0 on b goes to q1; q1 on b loops to q1; q1 on a goes to q2; q2 on b goes to q3; q2 on a goes back to q0; q3 on a goes to q2; q3 on b goes back to q1.

diagram.alt: A DFA with four states in a row. The first state is the start, the fourth is accepting. Reading a loops on the first state, b moves right; b loops on the second, a moves right; the third moves right on b; the fourth goes back to the third on a and to the second on b; the third goes back to the first on a.

solutionDiagram.alt: The same four-state DFA with states named by the longest suffix read so far that is a prefix of bab: empty, b, ba, bab. The state bab accepts, so the DFA accepts strings that end with bab.

options: The set of all strings containing an even number of $b$'s.
The set of all strings containing the pattern $bab$.
The set of all strings ending with the pattern $bab$.
The set of all strings not containing the pattern $aba$.

steps.title: What the question means by language, contain and end
steps.body: A DFA accepts a string if, starting in the start state and following one arrow per symbol, it finishes in an accepting state. 'Containing the pattern $bab$' means $bab$ appears somewhere inside the string; 'ending with $bab$' means the last three symbols are $bab$. A good way to read a DFA: give every state a meaning, the fact about the input that the state remembers, and check that each arrow keeps the meaning true. The rule used here: the language of a DFA is the set of inputs that lead to an accepting state, so compare each option with what the accepting state means.

steps.title: Give each state a meaning
steps.body: Name the states by the longest suffix of the input so far that is a prefix of $bab$: $q_0$ means none (empty), $q_1$ means $b$, $q_2$ means $ba$, $q_3$ means $bab$. Check the arrows. From $q_0$: $a$ gives suffix empty (stay), $b$ gives $b$ ($q_1$). From $q_1$ ($b$): $b$ gives $bb$, suffix $b$ (stay); $a$ gives $ba$ ($q_2$). From $q_2$ ($ba$): $b$ gives $bab$ ($q_3$); $a$ gives $baa$, no suffix (back to $q_0$). From $q_3$ ($bab$): $a$ gives $baba$, suffix $ba$ ($q_2$); $b$ gives $babb$, suffix $b$ ($q_1$). All eight arrows match the meaning, and $q_3$ is the only accepting state.

steps.title: The language is 'ends with bab'
steps.body: The DFA is in $q_3$ after reading the input exactly when the longest suffix that is a prefix of $bab$ is all of $bab$, that is, when the input ends with $bab$. So option (C) is correct. Note that $q_3$ does not trap the machine (it leaves on both symbols), so the DFA does not remember that $bab$ appeared earlier; that is the difference from 'contains'.

steps.title: Why the other options fail
steps.body: (A) The empty string has zero $b$'s, which is even, but the DFA rejects it (it stays in $q_0$); also $bab$ has two $b$'s and is accepted. (B) $baba$ contains $bab$ but ends in $q_2$, so it is rejected. (D) The empty string contains no $aba$ yet is rejected. A script that tests every string up to length 9 against all four options finds a mismatch for (A), (B) and (D) and none for (C). The answer is (C).

shortcut.body: The only way into the accepting state is $q_2\xrightarrow{b}q_3$, and the only way into $q_2$ is $q_1\xrightarrow{a}$, and into $q_1$ is $b$: so the last three symbols are $bab$. Confirm with two tests: the empty string is rejected, which kills (A) and (D) (both contain it), and $baba$ is rejected, which kills (B). About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing (A) from a quick glance at the two loops on $b$ and $a$. The empty string has zero $b$'s, which is even, but the DFA rejects it, and $bb$ has two $b$'s but ends in $q_1$, so it is rejected too.
Choosing (B) because the accepting state is reached through $bab$. After $bab$ one more $a$ leaves the accepting state, so strings like $baba$ that contain $bab$ are rejected.

Rejecting (C) because the accepting state $q_3$ has outgoing arrows and looks like it should trap the machine. It does not: the DFA accepts exactly when the last three symbols are $bab$, which is 'ends with', and $babab$ is accepted again after leaving $q_3$.
Choosing (D) because $aba$ does not appear on the path to the accepting state. The empty string contains no $aba$ and must then be accepted, but the DFA rejects it.

recognize.clues: A drawn DFA with four states in a row and one accepting state entered by arrows reading b, then a, then b. The options differ on 'contains', 'ends with' and a parity condition on b.
recognize.contrast: A 'contains' language needs an accepting state that traps the machine once the pattern appears. Here the accepting state has arrows to non-accepting states, so the machine forgets earlier matches, which is the sign of an 'ends with' language.

check.body: Run $babab$: the states are $q_0,q_1,q_2,q_3,q_2,q_3$, so it is accepted and it ends with $bab$. Run $baba$: it ends in $q_2$ and is rejected, although it contains $bab$. These two runs separate 'ends with' from 'contains'.

questions.stem: Which one of the following regular expressions is equivalent to the language accepted by the DFA given below?
questions.figure: Two states. The left state is the start state and is not accepting; the right state is accepting (double circle). The left state loops on 0; the left state goes to the right state on 1; the right state loops on 0; the right state goes back to the left state on 1.

solutionDiagram.alt: The two-state DFA with the left state named even and the right state odd, meaning the number of 1s read so far is even or odd; the accepted language is the strings with an odd number of 1s, written 0*1(0+10*1)*.

steps.title: What the DFA and a regular expression mean
steps.body: A DFA accepts the strings that lead from its start state to an accepting state. A regular expression describes a language with three operations: $+$ is 'or', juxtaposition is 'followed by', and $^*$ is 'zero or more repetitions'. Two expressions are equivalent when they describe the same set of strings. The practical rule: first say in words what the DFA remembers, then build the expression by following the paths, then test the options on a few short strings.

steps.title: Say in words what the DFA does
steps.body: Reading 0 never changes the state; reading 1 always switches between the two states. The start state is the left one, so the left state means an even number of 1's read so far and the right state means an odd number. The right state accepts. Therefore the DFA accepts exactly the strings with an odd number of 1's.

steps.title: Build the expression from the paths
steps.body: From the start state, any number of 0's stay there: $0^*$. The first 1 moves to the accepting state: $0^*1$. At the accepting state we may repeat any of two loops: read a 0 (stay), or read a 1 (go to the left state), read any number of 0's there, and read another 1 to come back: $10^*1$. So the repeated part is $(0+10^*1)^*$. The whole language is shown below, which is option (A).

steps.title: Test the other options
steps.body: The language has an odd number of 1's, so $\epsilon$ must be rejected and $1$ and $111$ accepted. (B) $0^*(10^*11)^*0^*$ accepts $\epsilon$ (zero repetitions), so it is not the language; also each repetition holds three 1's, so only counts that are multiples of 3 appear. (C) $0^*1(010^*1)^*0^*$ needs a 0 before each repeated block, so it rejects $111$. (D) $0(1+0^*10^*1)^*0^*$ must start with 0, so it rejects $1$. A script comparing each expression with the DFA on every string up to length 12 confirms that only (A) is equivalent.

shortcut.body: Read the language as 'odd number of 1's'. Test $\epsilon$, $1$ and $111$: $\epsilon$ must be rejected, so (B) is out; $1$ must be accepted, so (D) is out (it starts with 0); $111$ must be accepted, so (C) is out (each repeat needs a 0). Only (A) survives. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing (B) because it has the 'return to the start by two 1's' flavor. Each block $10^*11$ holds three 1's and the empty choice matches $\epsilon$, so it describes multiples of 3 ones, not an odd count.
Choosing (C) after matching the loop at the accepting state as 'read 0, then go around'. The 0 is inside the repeated block here, so a string like $111$ cannot be produced.
Choosing (D) by mistaking the first transition: the start state loops on 0 but the regular expression forces a leading 0, rejecting the accepted string $1$.

recognize.clues: A small DFA drawn in the question, a request for an equivalent regular expression, and four options that differ only in where the stars and the leading symbols sit.
recognize.contrast: Arden's theorem solves the same problem by algebra on state equations. With only two states, reading the paths and testing short strings is quicker and less error prone.

check.body: Run two strings through both the DFA and the chosen expression. The string 0110 has two 1s, so the DFA ends in the start state and rejects it, and the expression cannot split it as 0, 1, then a block 0 or 10*1. The string 01101 has three 1s, so the DFA accepts it, and the expression reads it as 0, 1, then the block 10*1 once.

questions.stem: Let $M$ be the 5-state NFA with $\epsilon$-transitions shown in the diagram below. Which one of the following regular expressions represents the language accepted by $M$ ?
questions.figure: Five states numbered 1 to 5; state 1 is the start state; states 2 and 5 are accepting. Transitions: 1 to 2 on epsilon; 1 to 4 on epsilon; 2 to 3 on 0; 3 to 2 on 0; 3 to 5 on epsilon; 4 to 5 on 1; 5 to 4 on 1.

diagram.alt: Five-state NFA: state 1 (start) has epsilon arrows to the accepting state 2 and to state 4; states 2 and 3 are joined by 0 in both directions; state 3 has an epsilon arrow to the accepting state 5; states 4 and 5 are joined by 1 in both directions.

solutionDiagram.alt: The NFA with each branch annotated: the top branch from state 1 to 2 and 3 gives (00)* and 0(00)*(11)* through the epsilon arrow to 5; the bottom branch through 4 and 5 gives 1(11)*.

steps.title: NFA, epsilon-transition and how to read the language
steps.body: An NFA accepts a string if some path from the start state, reading exactly that string, ends in an accepting state. An $\epsilon$-transition is a free move that reads no symbol, so the machine may take it at any time. To get a regular expression, list every kind of path from the start to an accepting state and write each as an expression; the language is their union (written $+$). The rule: a state that is not accepting contributes nothing by itself.

steps.title: Trace the top branch
steps.body: State 1 reaches state 2 for free, and state 2 is accepting. States 2 and 3 are joined by 0 in both directions, so after an even number of 0's we are in 2 and after an odd number in 3. So the strings $(00)^*$ end in 2 and are accepted. After $0(00)^*$ we are in 3, which moves for free to state 5, an accepting state, so these are accepted too. From 5 we can also read 1 to state 4 and 1 back to 5, and state 5 is accepting while 4 is not, so after $0(00)^*$ we may append $(11)^*$. This branch gives $(00)^*$ and $0(00)^*(11)^*$.

steps.title: Trace the bottom branch
steps.body: State 1 reaches state 4 for free; 4 is not accepting. Reading 1 moves to 5, which is accepting, and every further pair $11$ goes 5 to 4 and back to 5. So the bottom branch gives $1(11)^*$, strings of an odd number of 1's. The state 4 on its own accepts nothing, so the empty string comes only from the top branch.

steps.title: Combine and match
steps.body: The language is $(00)^*+0(00)^*(11)^*+1(11)^*$. Option (B) is $0^*+(1+0(00)^*)(11)^*$. Split $0^*=(00)^*+0(00)^*$ and expand $(1+0(00)^*)(11)^*=1(11)^*+0(00)^*(11)^*$. The term $0(00)^*$ is already inside $0(00)^*(11)^*$ (take zero repeats of $(11)$), so (B) equals our language. A script running the NFA and each option on all strings up to length 14 confirms that only (B) is equivalent. The other three each miss a string: (A) and (C) reject the single 0, which $M$ accepts ($1\to2\to3\to5$), and (D) rejects the empty string, which $M$ accepts (state 2).

shortcut.body: Test two short strings on the NFA. The empty string is accepted (1 reaches the accepting state 2 for free) and so is the single 0 (1, 2, 3 on 0, then 5 for free). Now see which options match both: (A) rejects 0, (C) rejects 0, (D) rejects $\epsilon$ because $0^+$ needs at least one 0 and the other terms start with a symbol. Only (B) matches both. About 1 minute. Safe, because each wrong option fails one of the two tests.

traps.text: Choosing (A) by forgetting the free move from 3 to 5: a single 0 reaches state 3 and then the accepting state 5, so 0 is accepted, but (A) allows only an even number of 0's.
Choosing (C) because $(00)^*$ in the middle looks like the top loop. It lets an even number of 0's precede $(11)^*$, but misses the odd number of 0's that moves to state 3 and then to 5.
Choosing (D) because $0^+$ looks like 'one or more zeros'. It misses the empty string, which is accepted since the start state moves for free to the accepting state 2.

recognize.clues: An NFA with epsilon moves leaving the start state into two separate cycles, and options that are unions of starred terms such as $(00)^*$ and $(11)^*$.
recognize.contrast: Subset construction would first remove the epsilon moves by building a DFA. Here the two branches read off directly as expressions, so no conversion is needed.

check.body: Trace 011 on the NFA: state 1 to 2 for free, 0 to state 3, a free move to state 5, then 1 to state 4 and 1 back to state 5, which is accepting. So 011 is in the language, and the chosen expression generates it as 0 followed by the pair 11. The string 11 alone must be rejected: it ends in state 4 and the expression has no 0 to supply for it.

questions.stem: Let $L_1$ be the language represented by the regular expression $b^*ab^*(ab^*ab^*)^*$ and $L_2 = \{ w \in (a+b)^* \mid |w| \le 4 \}$, where $|w|$ denotes the length of string $w$. The number of strings in $L_2$ which are also in $L_1$ is __________

steps.title: Reading a regular expression and counting what it describes
steps.body: A regular expression describes strings built by three operations: juxtaposition ('followed by'), $+$ ('or') and $^*$ ('zero or more repetitions'). $|w|$ is the length of $w$. $L_2$ is every string over $\{a,b\}$ of length at most 4, which includes the empty string, and the question asks how many of them are in $L_1$. The rule: first turn the expression into a plain property of strings, then count strings of each length with that property.

steps.title: Decode L1: an odd number of a's
steps.body: In $b^*ab^*(ab^*ab^*)^*$ the first part $b^*ab^*$ contains exactly one $a$, and each repetition of $(ab^*ab^*)$ adds exactly two $a$'s. So every string of $L_1$ has $1+2k$ a's, an odd number, with any number of $b$'s anywhere. Conversely every string with an odd number of $a$'s has this shape: put the first $a$ in the first part and group the remaining $a$'s in pairs. So $L_1=\{w\in\{a,b\}^*:\#_a(w)\ \text{is odd}\}$.

steps.title: Count by length
steps.body: For length $k$, choose which positions hold $a$; the number of choices with an odd count of $a$'s is the number of odd-sized subsets of $k$ positions, $2^{k-1}$ for $k\ge1$ (and 0 for $k=0$, since $\epsilon$ has zero $a$'s). Length 1: 1 (just $a$). Length 2: $\binom21=2$. Length 3: $\binom31+\binom33=4$. Length 4: $\binom41+\binom43=8$. The total is $1+2+4+8=15$. A script that matches the expression against all 31 strings of length at most 4 finds 15.

shortcut.body: Decode the expression as 'an odd number of a's', and use the fact that exactly half of the $2^k$ strings of each length $k\ge1$ have an odd number of $a$'s: $2^{k-1}$. The sum for $k=1,\dots,4$ is $2^4-1=15$. About 1 minute. Safe once the decoding is right; if the decoding slips (for example reading the expression as 'at least one $a$'), the count changes.

traps.text: 16: counting the empty string. $\epsilon$ has no $a$ and cannot match $b^*ab^*\cdots$, which needs an $a$ at least once.
31: counting every string of length at most 4. 26: counting every string that has at least one $a$. Only strings with an odd number of $a$'s match, and there are 15 of them.
8: counting only the length-4 strings. The question is for lengths up to 4, so shorter strings count as well.

recognize.clues: An expression paired with a length bound, and a question that asks how many strings of the bounded set also lie in the expression: decode the expression into a property, then count by length.
recognize.contrast: A two-state DFA for the same property describes the same language. The DFA view is useful for proofs, but the property view is what makes the per-length count easy.

check.body: Count the complement instead. There are $2^5-1=31$ strings of length at most 4 in total. Those with an even number of a's, including the empty string, number $1+1+2+4+8=16$ ($\epsilon$, then $2^{k-1}$ for each length $k\ge1$). Then $31-16=15$ strings have an odd number of a's.

questions.stem: Let $L_1, L_2$ be two regular languages and $L_3$ a language which is not regular. Which of the following statements is/are always TRUE?

steps.title: The vocabulary: complement, closure, 'always true'
steps.body: The complement $\overline{L}$ of a language over the alphabet $\Sigma$ is $\Sigma^*\setminus L$, all strings not in $L$. Regular languages are closed under complement, union and intersection: the result of these operations on regular languages is regular. A statement is 'always true' only when it holds for every choice of $L_1,L_2,L_3$ that fits the description, so one counterexample is enough to reject it, and an 'if and only if' needs both directions.

steps.title: Options (A) and (B) fail
steps.body: (A): The direction 'equal implies empty intersection' is fine, but $L_1\cap\overline{L_2}=\emptyset$ only says every string of $L_1$ is in $L_2$, that is $L_1\subseteq L_2$. Over $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$ take $L_1=\{a\}$ and $L_2=\{a,b\}$: the intersection is empty but $L_1\ne L_2$. (B): take $L_1=\Sigma^*$ (regular). Then $L_1\cup L_3=\Sigma^*$ is regular for every $L_3$, so the statement is not always true.

steps.title: Options (C) and (D) hold
steps.body: (C): suppose $\overline{L_3}$ were regular. Regular languages are closed under complement, so $\overline{\overline{L_3}}=L_3$ would be regular, contradicting the choice of $L_3$. So $\overline{L_3}$ is not regular. (D): by De Morgan, $\overline{L_1}\cup\overline{L_2}=\overline{L_1\cap L_2}$, and the intersection of regular languages is regular, and so is its complement. So (D) is regular. The answer is (C) and (D).

shortcut.body: Complementing is reversible, so a language is regular exactly when its complement is: (C) is true. (D) is just closure. For (A) and (B) try tiny languages: $\{a\}\subset\{a,b\}$ breaks (A), and $\Sigma^*\cup L_3=\Sigma^*$ breaks (B). About 1 minute.

traps.text: Choosing (A) by reading the empty intersection as equality. $L_1\cap\overline{L_2}=\emptyset$ gives only $L_1\subseteq L_2$; equality also needs $L_2\cap\overline{L_1}=\emptyset$.
Choosing (B) because a non-regular language 'spoils' any union. It does not when the regular part swallows it, for example $L_1=\Sigma^*$.
Leaving out (C) because the complement of a non-regular language seems like it could be tidy. Complement is its own inverse, so if the complement were regular, so would be the original.
Leaving out (D) after thinking the union of two complements is not covered by closure. De Morgan turns it into the complement of the intersection, which is regular.

recognize.clues: The phrase "always TRUE" with regular and non-regular languages mixed together, and options built from union, complement and an if-and-only-if claim.
recognize.contrast: The pumping lemma proves that a specific language is non-regular. Here the non-regularity of $L_3$ is given, so closure arguments and one counterexample per statement are enough.

check.body: Use different languages from the steps, over $\{a,b\}$. Take $L_3=\{ww\mid w\in\Sigma^*\}$ (not regular) and $L_1=\Sigma^*$: the union is $\Sigma^*$, regular, so a union with a non-regular language need not be non-regular. Take $L_1=\emptyset$ and $L_2=\{a\}$: $L_1\cap\overline{L_2}=\emptyset$ yet $L_1\ne L_2$, so the equivalence fails. For the two that hold, take $L_1=\{a\}$, $L_2=\{b\}$: $\overline{L_1}\cup\overline{L_2}=\Sigma^*$ is regular, as De Morgan predicts.

questions.stem: Consider the 5-state DFA $M$ accepting the language $L(M) \subset (0+1)^*$ shown below. For any string $w \in (0+1)^*$ let $n_0(w)$ be the number of $0$'s in $w$ and $n_1(w)$ be the number of $1$'s in $w$. Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
questions.figure: Five states numbered 1 to 5; state 1 is the start state and the only accepting state. Transitions: 1 on 0 to 2; 1 on 1 to 4; 2 on 0 to 3; 2 on 1 to 1; 3 on 0 to 1; 3 on 1 to 2; 4 on 0 to 1; 4 on 1 to 5; 5 on 0 to 4; 5 on 1 to 1.

diagram.alt: Five-state DFA. State 1 is the start and accepting state. Reading 0 from 1 goes to 2, then 3, then back to 1; reading 1 from 1 goes to 4, then 5, then back to 1; the opposite symbol steps backward along each chain.

solutionDiagram.alt: The minimal DFA with three states: state 1; the merged state 2,5; and the merged state 3,4. Reading 0 goes 1 to 2,5 to 3,4 to 1; reading 1 goes 1 to 3,4 to 2,5 to 1. State 1 is the start and accepts.

options: Any string $w$ with $n_0(w) = n_1(w)$ is in $L(M)$

steps.title: Distinguishable and equivalent states
steps.body: Two states $p$ and $q$ are distinguishable if some string $z$ makes exactly one of them end in an accepting state when started from it; otherwise they are equivalent and a minimal DFA merges them. A state is accepting or not on the empty string, so an accepting state is distinguishable from every non-accepting state. The table-filling method then marks a pair as distinguishable if on some symbol the successors are already a marked pair. Pairs that never get marked are equivalent. The question asks for the FALSE statements.

steps.title: Fill the table
steps.body: Successors written as (on 0, on 1): state 2 is (3, 1), state 3 is (1, 2), state 4 is (1, 5), state 5 is (4, 1). State 1 is the only accepting state, so it is distinguishable from 2, 3, 4, 5. Pair (2,3): on 0 the successors are (3,1), and 1 is accepting while 3 is not, so marked. Pair (2,4): on 0, (3,1), marked. Pair (3,5): on 0, (1,4), marked. Pair (4,5): on 0, (1,4), marked. Pair (3,4): on 0 both go to 1, on 1 they go to (2,5). Pair (2,5): on 0 they go to (3,4), on 1 both go to 1. So (3,4) and (2,5) point only at each other and at identical states: neither is ever marked, and both pairs are equivalent.

steps.title: What the three classes mean
steps.body: The classes are $\{1\}$, $\{2,5\}$ and $\{3,4\}$. Reading 0 adds 1 and reading 1 subtracts 1 from $d=(n_0-n_1)\bmod 3$: $d=0$ is state 1, $d=1$ is states 2 and 5, $d=2$ is states 3 and 4 (reading 1 from state 1 gives $-1\equiv2$, state 4). Only $d=0$ is accepting. A script confirms the classes and that $L(M)=\{w:\ n_0(w)-n_1(w)\equiv0\pmod 3\}$.

steps.title: Judge the four statements
steps.body: (A) States 2 and 4 are in different classes ($d=1$ against $d=2$): distinguishable, for example by the string $0$: from 2 it goes to 3, from 4 it goes to 1 (accepting). Statement (A) is true. (B) States 3 and 4 are the same class: not distinguishable, so (B) is false. (C) States 2 and 5 are the same class: so (C) is false. (D) If $n_0=n_1$ then the difference is $0$, so the string lands in state 1 and is accepted: true. The false statements are (B) and (C).

shortcut.body: Spot that 3 and 4 both go to 1 on 0, and 2 and 5 both go to 1 on 1, while (3,4) go to (2,5) on 1 and (2,5) go to (3,4) on 0. The pairs depend only on each other and on equal targets, so they never separate: (B) and (C) are false. (D) holds because 0 and 1 cancel each other in the count. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Marking (A) false because states 2 and 4 both have an arrow to state 1. They reach it on different symbols (2 on 1, 4 on 0), and the string $0$ separates them.
Marking (D) false by thinking equal counts could still fail. The state tracks $n_0-n_1 \bmod 3$, and equal counts give difference 0, which is the accepting state.
Taking 3 and 4 as distinguishable because they are different circles with different arrows into them. Their outgoing behavior is the same, so they are merged in the minimal DFA.
Taking 2 and 5 as distinguishable for the same reason. Both go to state 1 on 1 and to the merged class $\{3,4\}$ on 0.

recognize.clues: The word "distinguishable" in the statements, and a five-state DFA for a language that looks like it needs fewer states, so a pairwise table-filling test applies.
recognize.contrast: Myhill-Nerode counts the classes through the prefixes of strings. Table filling decides the specific pairs of states, which is exactly what each statement here asks.

check.body: Look for a separating string between states 3 and 4 directly. From 3 and from 4 the string 0 reaches state 1 for both. The string 11 goes 3 to 2 to 1 and 4 to 5 to 1, again both accepting. The string 01 ends in state 4 for both, which rejects. No short string separates them, which fits their being equivalent.

questions.stem: Consider the following two regular expressions over the alphabet $\{0,1\}$: $r = 0^* + 1^*$ and $s = 01^* + 10^*$. The total number of strings of length less than or equal to 5, which are neither in $r$ nor in $s$, is __________

steps.title: Decode the two expressions
steps.body: In a regular expression, $+$ means 'or' and $^*$ means 'zero or more repetitions', and juxtaposition means 'followed by'. So $r=0^*+1^*$ describes the strings that are all 0's or all 1's, including the empty string. $s=01^*+10^*$ describes a 0 followed by any number of 1's, or a 1 followed by any number of 0's. We count the strings of length at most 5 that are in neither, so we count those in $r$ or $s$ and subtract from the total.

steps.title: Count the strings in r or s, length by length
steps.body: Length 0: only $\epsilon$ (from $0^*$), 1 string. Length 1: the strings $0$ and $1$ are in $r$, and also in $s$ ($0\cdot1^0$ and $1\cdot0^0$), so just 2 strings, counted once. Length 2: $r$ gives $00,11$ and $s$ gives $01,10$: 4 strings, all four. Length $k\ge3$: $r$ gives $0^k,1^k$ and $s$ gives $01^{k-1},10^{k-1}$, four distinct strings. So the counts are $1,2,4,4,4,4$ for lengths $0$ to $5$, a total of $19$.

steps.title: Subtract from all strings
steps.body: There are $2^0+2^1+\dots+2^5=63$ strings of length at most 5. Those in neither expression: $63-19=44$. Per length this is $2^k-4$ for $k\ge3$, that is $4+12+28=44$, and 0 for lengths 0, 1, 2 (every string of those lengths is in $r$ or $s$). A script that matches both expressions against all 63 strings gives 44.

shortcut.body: Every string of length 0, 1 or 2 is in $r\cup s$. For $k\ge3$ exactly four strings of each length are in $r\cup s$ ($0^k$, $1^k$, $01^{k-1}$, $10^{k-1}$), so $2^k-4$ are outside: $4+12+28=44$. About 1.5 minutes. Safe, as long as the distinctness of the four strings for $k\ge3$ is checked.

traps.text: 45: forgetting that $\epsilon$ belongs to $0^*$, which leaves out one string and lowers the count of strings in $r\cup s$ to 18.
43: counting $0$ and $1$ twice at length 1, once for $r$ and once for $s$, which gives 20 strings in $r\cup s$ instead of 19.
19: answering with the number of strings that are in $r$ or $s$, instead of those in neither.

recognize.clues: The phrase "neither in $r$ nor in $s$" with a length bound: a complement count over the union of two expressions that each describe a simple family of strings.
recognize.contrast: Closure under union and complement tells you the result is regular but says nothing about its size. To count, take all strings minus the union, length by length.

check.body: Check one length directly. For length 3 there are 8 strings. The ones in $r$ or $s$ are 000, 111, 011 and 100, so 4 are outside: 001, 010, 101 and 110. This agrees with the per-length count for $k=3$.

variation.explanation: For length $k\ge1$, $r$ and $s$ each hold $k+1$ strings and share exactly $0^k$ and $1^k$, so the union has $2k$ strings. Length 0 has one. The union totals $1+2+4+6+8+10=31$, and all strings of length at most 5 number 63, so $63-31=32$ lie in neither.

questions.stem: Consider the Deterministic Finite-state Automaton (DFA) $\mathcal{A}$ shown below. The DFA runs on the alphabet $\{0,1\}$, and has the set of states $\{s,p,q,r\}$, with $s$ being the start state and $p$ being the only final state. Which one of the following regular expressions correctly describes the language accepted by $\mathcal{A}$?
questions.figure: Transitions: s on 1 to p; s on 0 to r; p on 0 to p; p on 1 to q; q on 1 to p; q on 0 to r; r on 0 to r; r on 1 to r. State s is the start state and p is the only final state. Once the automaton enters r it can never leave.

diagram.alt: DFA with states s, p, q, r. The start state s goes to the final state p on 1 and to r on 0. State p loops on 0 and goes to q on 1; q returns to p on 1 and goes to r on 0; r loops on 0 and 1.

solutionDiagram.alt: The same DFA annotated: after the first 1 the closed walks at p are the loop 0 and the round trip p to q to p reading 11; every other move falls into the dead state r. The language is 1(0 + 11)*.

steps.title: What a regular expression for an automaton means
steps.body: A DFA accepts a string when the single path that the string traces from the start state ends in a final state. A regular expression for the DFA must therefore generate exactly the labels of the paths that run from the start state to a final state. A state from which no final state can be reached is a dead state: any string that enters it is rejected, so its edges can be ignored when writing the expression. The star $R^*$ means any number of repetitions of $R$, including none.

steps.title: Find the dead state and the first step
steps.body: From $r$ the automaton only loops back to $r$, and $r$ is not final, so $r$ is dead. That removes the edge $s \xrightarrow{0} r$ and the edge $q \xrightarrow{0} r$. The only live move from $s$ is $s \xrightarrow{1} p$, so every accepted string starts with $1$ and then sits at $p$.

steps.title: List the closed walks at p
steps.body: After the first $1$, the automaton is at $p$, the only final state. A string is accepted when it ends at $p$, so what follows is any number of closed walks that start and end at $p$. The two simple ones are the loop that reads $0$, and the round trip $p \to q \to p$ that reads $1$ then $1$, which is $11$. From $q$ the symbol $0$ leads to the dead state, so no other walk is possible.

steps.title: Check the options against short strings
steps.body: The string $10$ goes $s \to p \to p$ and is accepted. Option (A) $1(0^*11)^*$ needs every $0$ to be followed later by $11$, so it rejects $10$. Option (D) $1(110^*)^*$ forces $11$ before any $0$, so it also rejects $10$. Option (B) starts with $0$, which sends $\mathcal{A}$ to the dead state, so it cannot describe $L$; it rejects $1$, which $\mathcal{A}$ accepts. Option (C) is the expression just derived. The answer is (C).

shortcut.body: Run the one-symbol-after-1 test: the string $10$ is accepted by the DFA ($s \to p \to p$). Options (A) and (D) reject it and option (B) cannot start with $0$ at all, so (C) is left. About 30 seconds. It is safe here because only (C) lets a lone $0$ follow the first $1$.

traps.text: Choosing $1(0^*11)^*$ by reading the round trip as $0^*11$. The loop on $p$ reads a single $0$ by itself, so $0$ is a separate alternative, not a prefix of $11$.
Choosing $0(0+1)^*$ because $0$ is the first symbol of the drawing label. The start state sends $0$ to the dead state $r$, so no accepted string starts with $0$.
Choosing $1(110^*)^*$ by putting the loop on $0$ after the $11$. The $0$-loop is at $p$ and can be taken at any time, for example straight after the first $1$.

recognize.clues: A four-state DFA with one sink state and a single final state, and options of the form "first symbol, then a starred group".
recognize.contrast: Arden's theorem would solve the state equations algebraically. With a dead state and one final state, listing the closed walks at the final state is shorter.

check.body: Test the string 1011. The DFA goes s to p, p to p on 0, p to q on 1 and q to p on 1, so it is accepted. The chosen expression reads it as 1, then 0, then 11. The string 101 ends in q, so the DFA rejects it, and the expression cannot split it because a lone 1 after the leading 1 never completes the pair.

A state from which no accepting state can be reached is dead. Edges into it are deleted when you read off the language.

After the first live move you are at the accepting state. Which sequences of labels start at p and come back to p, without passing through the dead state?
State s has a single live edge, which goes to p, and its other edge goes to the dead state. So only one symbol can start an accepted string.

questions.stem: Consider the following definition of a lexical token $\mathbf{id}$ for an identifier in a programming language, using extended regular expressions. Which one of the following Non-deterministic Finite-state Automata with $\epsilon$-transitions accepts the set of valid identifiers? (A double-circle denotes a final state)
questions.figure: Each option is an NFA with start state 0 and an arrow labelled letter leaving it for state 1; the drawing numbers the states. (A) States 0 and 1; state 1 is final; 0 goes to 1 on letter and also on $\epsilon$; state 1 loops on letter and on digit. (B) State 1 is final and has $\epsilon$ moves to final states 2 and 3; state 2 loops on letter, state 3 loops on digit. (C) State 1 is final; 1 goes by $\epsilon$ to 2 and to 4; 2 goes to 3 on letter; 4 goes to 5 on digit; 3 and 5 each go by $\epsilon$ to 6; 6 goes by $\epsilon$ back to 1. (D) State 1 is final; 1 goes to 2 on letter; 2 goes to 3 on digit; 3 goes by $\epsilon$ back to 1.

diagram.alt: Four epsilon-NFAs labelled A to D. All start with a letter arrow from state 0 to state 1. A adds an epsilon arrow beside it and a loop on letter and digit; B has two epsilon moves to separate loops for letter and digit; C has two parallel letter and digit branches joined by epsilon and returned to state 1; D has a letter then digit chain returned to state 1 by epsilon.

options: (A) letter takes the start state to the final state, and an $\epsilon$ arrow also joins them; the final state loops on letter and on digit
(B) after letter, two $\epsilon$ moves reach two final states; one loops on letter and the other loops on digit
(C) after letter, $\epsilon$ moves reach a letter branch and a digit branch that rejoin and return by $\epsilon$ to the final state
(D) after letter, the final state continues with letter then digit and returns by $\epsilon$ to itself

steps.title: What an epsilon-NFA accepts
steps.body: An NFA with $\epsilon$-transitions may follow an $\epsilon$ arrow without reading any symbol. A string is accepted when some path labelled by the string, with any number of free $\epsilon$ moves, ends in a final state. Here the alphabet symbols are the two token classes letter and digit, and the definition says an identifier is one letter followed by any number of letters or digits in any order.

steps.title: What the automaton must do
steps.body: It must accept a lone letter, so the state reached after the first letter is final. From that final state, each further symbol must be a letter or a digit, and after that symbol the machine must be able to accept again and read yet another letter or digit. It must reject the empty string and any string that starts with a digit.

steps.title: Reject A, B and D
steps.body: (A) The $\epsilon$ arrow lets the start state reach the final state with no input, so the empty string is accepted, and the string digit is accepted through the loop on digit. Neither is an identifier. (B) After the first letter the machine must pick one of the two $\epsilon$ branches, and the branches loop separately. It accepts letter letter and letter digit digit, but not letter letter digit, because once it chose the letter loop it cannot read a digit. It accepts letter followed by letters only, or by digits only. (D) After the first letter it can only read letter then digit, then return. It rejects letter letter, a valid identifier.

steps.title: Confirm C
steps.body: In (C) the final state 1 moves by $\epsilon$ into either branch. The upper branch reads one letter, the lower reads one digit, both rejoin at state 6, and $\epsilon$ leads back to state 1, which is final and can choose again. So after the first letter every further symbol, whichever class, returns to the final state. That generates exactly $\text{letter}(\text{letter}+\text{digit})^*$. The answer is (C).

shortcut.body: Three strings decide it: the empty string kills (A), letter letter kills (D), and letter letter digit kills (B). Only (C) survives. About 1 minute. The test strings are safe because each wrong option fails on a valid or an invalid identifier you can trace in two steps.

traps.text: Choosing (A) because the loop on letter and digit looks like the star. The $\epsilon$ arrow from the start state skips the compulsory first letter, so the empty string and digit-led strings are accepted.
Choosing (B) after reading the two loops as the union inside the star. Two separate loops give letter(letter*+digit*), which cannot mix letters and digits after the first letter.
Choosing (D) because it shows both letter and digit on the path. It forces them in pairs, so it rejects the valid identifier made of a letter followed by a single letter.

recognize.clues: Four epsilon-NFAs given as drawings and a token defined by alternation and a star: the test is which automaton accepts exactly the defined strings.
recognize.contrast: A DFA needs no epsilon moves. Here the epsilon arrows are what build the starred choice of letter or digit, so reading them as free jumps is the key skill.

check.body: Trace the string letter digit letter on the chosen automaton. State 0 reads letter to state 1, a free move reaches state 4, digit goes to 5, free moves reach 6 and then 1, then another free move to 2 and letter to 3, and free moves lead back to the final state 1. It is accepted, and the same pattern works for any longer mix.

The token is a letter followed by a loop over letters and digits. An NFA can build a loop with a self-loop or with a cycle that uses epsilon moves.
Test each automaton on short strings. It must accept a lone letter and a letter followed by any mix of letters and digits, and it must reject the empty string.

variation.stem: A token is defined by: letter is [A-Za-z], digit is [0-9], and lbl is letter digit* letter*, a letter, then any digits, then any letters. Each option is an NFA with epsilon moves, start state 0 and an arrow labelled letter from 0 to 1. Which NFA accepts exactly the valid lbl tokens?

questions.stem: Consider the language $L$ over the alphabet $\{0, 1\}$, given below: $L = \{w \in \{0,1\}^* \mid w \text{ does not contain three or more consecutive 1's}\}$. The minimum number of states in a Deterministic Finite-State Automaton (DFA) for $L$ is ____.

solutionDiagram.alt: DFA with four states: 0, 1 and 2 count the 1s at the end of the input so far and are all accepting; a third 1 moves to a non-accepting dead state that loops on 0 and 1. A 0 returns states 1 and 2 to state 0.

steps.title: How many states a DFA needs
steps.body: A DFA is a machine that remembers only which of its states it is in. Two prefixes $u$ and $v$ need different states exactly when some continuation $z$ makes one of $uz$, $vz$ belong to the language and the other not. This is the Myhill-Nerode idea. The minimum number of states equals the number of groups of prefixes that no continuation can tell apart.

steps.title: What the machine must remember
steps.body: To forbid $111$ the machine must know how many 1s end the input so far. That count is 0 when the input is empty or ends in 0, 1 after a single trailing 1, 2 after exactly two trailing 1s. A third 1 makes the string contain $111$ for ever, which is a fourth situation: dead. Older symbols do not matter, since a 0 resets the count.

steps.title: The four groups are pairwise distinguishable
steps.body: Count 0 and count 1 differ on the continuation $11$: from count 0 the string $11$ is allowed, from count 1 it creates $111$. Count 1 and count 2 differ on $1$. Count 0 and count 2 also differ on $1$. The dead group rejects every continuation, including the empty one, while the other three accept the empty continuation, so dead differs from all of them. Four groups, and four states are enough (the figure). So the minimum is 4.

shortcut.body: Forbidding $k$ consecutive 1s needs $k$ counter states $0,\dots,k-1$ plus one dead state, so $k=3$ gives $3+1=4$. About 30 seconds. This count is only for a single repeated symbol; for a mixed pattern such as 011 the states are the prefixes of the pattern, not a plain counter.

traps.text: Answering 3 by counting only the trailing-1 states. A DFA needs a move for every symbol in every state, so the third 1 needs a place to go: the dead state makes it 4.
Answering 5 by giving the start state its own group apart from the "ended in 0" group. Both have zero trailing 1s and accept exactly the same continuations, so they are one state.

recognize.clues: The question asks for the minimum number of DFA states for a language defined by a forbidden substring, "three or more consecutive 1's". A forbidden run means the machine only has to count the current run of 1s.
recognize.contrast: Do not use the subset construction or an NFA count here. The language is given by a property, not by an NFA, so the states come from what must be remembered (see minimization for the same count by indistinguishable prefixes).

check.body: Run the same reasoning on smaller bounds. Forbidding $11$ needs 3 states, forbidding a single $1$ leaves $0^*$ and needs 2, and a brute-force count of distinguishable prefixes for forbidding $111$ gives 4. Each bound $k$ costs $k+1$ states, so $k=3$ gives 4.
