hints.text: Ask what the machine must remember about the input so far to be able to reject a forbidden pattern. Everything else it can forget.
Two prefixes need different states only when some continuation is accepted after one but rejected after the other. Prefixes that no continuation can separate share a state.
A DFA needs a move on every symbol from every state, so a pattern that must be rejected for ever needs a place to go once it has appeared.
List the situations by how many 1s end the input so far, starting at none, and ask what the next 1 does in each. Do not forget the situation after the forbidden pattern.
Zero trailing 1s and one trailing 1 are already different: appending $11$ is safe from the first and fatal from the second. Keep separating the remaining situations this way.

variation.stem: Consider the language $L$ over the alphabet $\{0,1\}$ given by $L=\{w \mid w \text{ does not contain } 1111 \text{ as a substring}\}$. The minimum number of states in a complete DFA for $L$ is ____.
variation.explanation: Track the number of 1s ending the input: 0, 1, 2 or 3, all accepting. A fourth consecutive 1 sends the machine to a dead state that rejects for ever. These five groups are pairwise distinguishable, so 5 states are needed.

questions.stem: Which one of the following regular expressions correctly represents the language of the finite automaton given below?
questions.figure: Three states. The start state S is not final; A and B are final. S on a to A; S on b to B; A on b to S; A on b to A (a loop); B on a to S; B on a to B (a loop). A has two arrows on b and B has two arrows on a, so the automaton is nondeterministic. The drawing has no state names; S, A and B are ours.

diagram.alt: Nondeterministic automaton: the non-final start state S goes to the final state A on a and to the final state B on b. A goes back to S on b and loops on b; B goes back to S on a and loops on a.

solutionDiagram.alt: The same automaton with the language derived beneath it: the loops at S are a b* b through A and b a* a through B, and the last stretch ends in A or B with a b* or b a*, giving (a b* b + b a* a)* (a b* + b a*).

steps.title: Reading a language off a nondeterministic automaton
steps.body: A nondeterministic automaton accepts a string when at least one path labelled by the string runs from the start state to a final state. So the language is the set of path labels. A path that leaves a state and later comes back to it is a loop, and any number of loops can be repeated, which is what the star expresses. The plan: find the loops at the start state, then the way out to a final state.

steps.title: Loops from S back to S
steps.body: Through A: read $a$ to reach A, read any number of $b$ on the loop at A, then read one $b$ to return to S. That is $ab^*b$. Through B: read $b$, any number of $a$ on the loop at B, then one $a$ back to S: $ba^*a$. These are the only ways to come back to S, so any number of visits to S read $(ab^*b+ba^*a)^*$.

steps.title: The last stretch
steps.body: S is not final, so the string must end in A or B. After the last visit to S the path goes to A and stays there, reading $ab^*$, or goes to B and stays there, reading $ba^*$. The empty string is not accepted, since S is not final. Joining the two parts gives the language.

steps.title: Compare with the options
steps.body: This is option (D), with the two loop terms written in the other order. Option (A) rejects the accepted string $a$. Option (B) never mixes the two kinds of loop, so it rejects $abbaa$, which the automaton accepts by the path S, A, S, B, B, B (reading $a,b,b,a,a$). Option (C) ends with $a^*+b^*$, which includes the empty ending, so it accepts the empty string and $aa$, and the automaton accepts neither. The answer is (D).

shortcut.body: The empty string is rejected because S is not final, which removes (C), whose last factor can be empty. The single symbol $a$ is accepted (S to A) and (A) cannot produce it, and (B) cannot mix an A-loop with a B-loop. That leaves (D). About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing (A) after tracing only one trip out of S and back. It forgets that the automaton may stop in A or B, so it rejects short accepted strings such as $a$ and $b$.
Choosing (B) because each half looks like a star of one loop. The two sets of loops can alternate in one string, so a separate star for each does not cover $abbaa$.

Choosing (C) because its loop part is right. The ending $a^*+b^*$ is wrong: it can be empty, so the string may end at S, which is not final, and it accepts $aa$, which the automaton rejects because A has no move on $a$.

recognize.clues: The stem gives a finite automaton in a figure and asks which regular expression represents its language. The start state is not final and two states each have a self-loop, so the loops at the start state decide the shape of the expression.
recognize.contrast: This is not a closure or pumping question. Compare with Arden-style equations: they reach the same expression, but here reading the loops off the figure is faster.

check.body: Compare the strings of length 2. The automaton accepts exactly $ab$ and $ba$ (a path of two moves that stops in a final state), and rejects $aa$ and $bb$ because the side states have no move on that symbol. The correct option generates $ab$ and $ba$ and nothing else of length 2, which an enumeration confirms up to length 9.

variation.stem: An automaton has two states, S (start and final) and A. From S the symbol $a$ goes to A and the symbol $b$ has no move. From A the symbol $a$ goes to A and the symbol $b$ goes to S. Which regular expression represents the language it accepts?

questions.stem: Consider the following languages: $L_1 = \{a^n w a^n \mid w \in \{a,b\}^*\}$ and $L_2 = \{w x w^R \mid w, x \in \{a,b\}^*,\ |w|, |x| > 0\}$. Note that $w^R$ is the reversal of the string $w$. Which of the following is/are TRUE?
options: $L_1$ and $L_2$ are context-free but not regular.

steps.title: Definitions to keep in view
steps.body: A language is regular if a finite automaton accepts it and context-free if a pushdown automaton or a context-free grammar generates it. Every regular language is context-free, so any language that is regular satisfies both of these descriptions. A language is "context-free but not regular" only if it is context-free and also fails to be regular. The pattern $a^n \dots a^n$ and the pattern $w \dots w^R$ tempt one to expect unbounded counting or matching, so the first job is to see how much of that matching is really forced.

steps.title: L1 is all strings
steps.body: The definition lets $n$ be any non-negative integer, so $n=0$ is allowed. Then $a^0 w a^0 = w$ for any $w\in\{a,b\}^*$, which puts every string in $L_1$. Conversely every member of $L_1$ is a string over $\{a,b\}$. Hence $L_1=\{a,b\}^*$, which is regular.

steps.title: L2 depends only on the two end symbols
steps.body: Take $w$ of length 1, say $w=c$. Then $w^R=c$ and $wxw^R = c\,x\,c$ with $x$ any non-empty string, so every string of length at least 3 whose first and last symbols are equal belongs to $L_2$. Conversely, if $s=wxw^R$ with $|w|\ge 1$ and $|x|\ge 1$ then $|s|\ge 3$, and the first symbol of $s$ is the first symbol of $w$, which is the last symbol of $w^R$, which is the last symbol of $s$. So $L_2$ is exactly the strings of length at least 3 with equal first and last symbols, written as a regular expression below. That is regular.

steps.title: Judge the options
steps.body: Both languages are regular, so (A) is true. Regular languages are context-free, so (B) is true and (C) is true. (D) says the languages are not regular, which is false. The answer is (A), (B), (C).

shortcut.body: Set $n=0$ in $L_1$ and take $|w|=1$ in $L_2$: the matching conditions collapse, and both languages become regular. Then every "regular" and "context-free" statement is true and the "not regular" one is false. About 2 minutes. It is safe because the definition lets $n$ and $|w|$ take the smallest values.

traps.text: Choosing (D) because $a^nwa^n$ and $wxw^R$ resemble $a^nb^n$ and palindromes. The free middle part $w$ or $x$ absorbs everything, so no counting or full reversal is needed.
Leaving out (A) for fear that $L_2$ requires matching a whole reversed string. Only one symbol of $w$ has to match, because $w$ can have length 1.
Leaving out (B) after deciding the languages are regular and so not "context-free". Every regular language is also context-free, so both descriptions hold.
Leaving out (C) for the same reason. (C) is a true statement here: $L_1$ is regular, and $L_2$, being regular, is context-free.

recognize.clues: Both languages have a shape that suggests matching ($a^n\dots a^n$ and $w\dots w^R$), but each has a free part, $w$ or $x$, between the matched pieces. The task is to decide whether the matching is real or collapses.
recognize.contrast: Unlike $\{a^nb^n\}$, where the two counts are tied by nothing else, here $n=0$ and $|w|=1$ are allowed. Check the smallest parameter values before reaching for the pumping lemma.

check.body: Spot-check membership. With $n=0$, the string $ba$ is in $L_1$ ($w=ba$), so $L_1$ has no restriction at all. In $L_2$ the string $bab$ is a member ($w=b$, $x=a$) and $ab$ is not, since a member has length at least 3. A rule that only compares the first and last symbols fits every such test.

variation.stem: Let $L_1=\{0^n w 0^n \mid w\in\{0,1\}^*,\ n\ge 0\}$ and $L_2=\{0^n1^n \mid n\ge 0\}$. Which of the following is/are TRUE?

questions.stem: Let $L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$ be an arbitrary regular language accepted by a minimal DFA with $k$ states. Which one of the following languages must necessarily be accepted by a minimal DFA with $k$ states?

steps.title: What "minimal DFA" counts
steps.body: A minimal DFA for $L$ is a complete DFA (every state has a move on both symbols) with the fewest states. Its states correspond to the groups of strings that behave alike: two strings are in the same group when every continuation is accepted after both or rejected after both. In a minimal DFA any two states are told apart by some continuation that is accepted from one and rejected from the other. "Must necessarily" means the claim has to hold for every $L$, so a single counterexample rejects an option.

steps.title: The complement keeps k states
steps.body: Take the minimal DFA for $L$ and swap the final and non-final states, keeping every arrow. A string reaches the same state as before, but it is now accepted exactly when it was rejected, so this DFA accepts $\{0,1\}^*-L$. Two states that a continuation $z$ separated before are still separated by the same $z$, with the roles reversed. So all $k$ states are still pairwise distinguishable, and the DFA is minimal with $k$ states.
steps.tex: \overline{L}\ \text{has the same } k\ \text{states, with final states swapped}

steps.title: The other three can change the count
steps.body: For $L=\{0,1\}^*$ one state suffices ($k=1$), but $L-\{01\}$ needs 4: the groups of $\varepsilon$, $0$, $01$ and every other string. For $L=\emptyset$ ($k=1$), $L\cup\{01\}=\{01\}$ also needs 4 states. For $L$ equal to the strings of odd length ($k=2$), $L\cdot L$ is the strings of even length at least 2, which needs 3 states. The answer is (C).

shortcut.body: Complement only flips which states are final, so the state count cannot move. To kill the others, try the two smallest languages, $\{0,1\}^*$ and $\emptyset$, each with $k=1$: removing or adding $01$ forces extra states. About 1 minute. Safe, because the question asks for "must necessarily".

traps.text: Choosing $L-\{01\}$ because removing one string seems to leave the structure alone. For $L=\{0,1\}^*$ it grows from 1 state to 4.
Choosing $L\cup\{01\}$ for the same reason. Adding one string to $L=\emptyset$ takes the DFA from 1 state to 4.

Choosing $L\cdot L$ because concatenating with itself looks like a closure operation that preserves size. Closure does not mean the same state count: odd-length strings give $k=2$ but $L\cdot L$ needs 3.

recognize.clues: The stem fixes the size $k$ of a minimal DFA for an arbitrary regular $L$ and asks which derived language must keep that size. "Must necessarily" means every $L$, so the size of the minimal DFA under each operation is what is tested.
recognize.contrast: This is not a closure question: all four languages are regular. Closure tells you a DFA exists, minimization tells you how many states it needs.

check.body: Substitute $L$ = strings ending in 0, which has $k=2$. Its complement is the empty string plus the strings ending in 1, which also needs 2 states (last symbol is 0 or not, with the empty string grouped with ending in 1). Now take $L=\{0,1\}^*$ with $k=1$: the complement is empty and still has 1 state, while $L-\{01\}$ has 4.

A minimal DFA has one state for each group of strings that no continuation can tell apart, so its size is the number of such groups.
An operation keeps the state count only if the same distinguishing continuations still work afterwards. Ask of each operation what happens to the groups of strings.

variation.stem: A regular language $M\subseteq\{a,b\}^*$ has a minimal complete DFA with $n$ states. For which one of the following languages is a minimal DFA guaranteed to have exactly $n$ states, whatever $M$ is?
options: the language obtained from $M$ by exchanging every $a$ with $b$
variation.explanation: Exchanging $a$ and $b$ on the arrows of the minimal DFA gives a DFA for the new language with the same states, and every pair of states is still told apart by the exchanged continuation, so it stays minimal with $n$ states. The others can change the count: for $M=\{a,b\}^*$ ($n=1$), $M\cdot\{a\}$ needs 2 states, and $M\cap\{ab\}=\{ab\}$ needs 4; for $M=\emptyset$ ($n=1$), $M\cup\{\varepsilon\}=\{\varepsilon\}$ needs 2.

questions.stem: Consider the following deterministic finite automaton (DFA). The number of strings of length 8 accepted by the above automaton is ____.
questions.figure: Six states; the start state is s and F is the only final state. s on 0 to a; s on 1 to b; a on 0 to c; a on 1 to d; b on 0 to c; b on 1 to d; c on 0 and on 1 to F; d on 0 and on 1 to F; F on 0 and on 1 to F. The drawing has no state names; s, a to d and F are ours.

diagram.alt: DFA with start state s, middle states a and b, further states c and d, and final state F. Both a and b go to c on 0 and to d on 1; c and d go to F on both symbols; F loops on 0 and 1.

solutionDiagram.alt: The same DFA with a note that the path of every string has the same shape: after 3 symbols the machine is in F and stays there, so every string of length 3 or more is accepted, giving 2^8 = 256 strings of length 8.

steps.title: How a DFA counts accepted strings
steps.body: A DFA is deterministic: each string traces exactly one path from the start state, one symbol per move. The string is accepted if that path ends in a final state. To count the accepted strings of a given length, find which paths of that length end in a final state and how many strings produce each.

steps.title: Follow the first three symbols
steps.body: From $s$ the first symbol leads to $a$ or $b$. From $a$ and from $b$ the second symbol leads to $c$ (on 0) or $d$ (on 1). From $c$ and from $d$ both symbols lead to $F$. So after exactly three symbols every string is in $F$, whatever it is.

steps.title: F is absorbing
steps.body: State $F$ is final and loops on both 0 and 1, so once reached it is never left. Therefore every string of length 3 or more is accepted. A string of length 8 is accepted whatever its symbols are, so the number accepted is the number of binary strings of length 8.

shortcut.body: Count levels: 2 symbols reach $c$ or $d$, the third reaches $F$ with no choice, and $F$ loops. So nothing of length 8 is rejected: answer $2^8=256$. About 30 seconds. Safe because the machine is complete: every state has a move on both symbols.

traps.text: Answering 128 by assuming only the paths through one of $c$ or $d$ reach $F$. Both $c$ and $d$ lead to $F$ on either symbol.
Answering 8 by counting only the three-symbol prefixes that reach $F$. The remaining five symbols are free because $F$ loops on both.

recognize.clues: The stem gives a complete DFA in a figure and asks for the number of accepted strings of one fixed length. Because each state has a move on both symbols, each string follows exactly one path, so counting paths counts strings.
recognize.contrast: This is not a minimization or design question: the automaton is given. It is also not an NFA count, where one string can have several paths and counting paths would overcount.

check.body: Count the rejected strings instead. A string is rejected only if it ends in a non-final state, but the non-final states are visited only in the first two moves, and from the third move on the machine is in the final state. So no string of length 8 is rejected, and the accepted count is $2^8=256$.

variation.stem: Consider a DFA with states s (start), a, b, c, F (the only final state) and D. From s the symbol 0 goes to a and the symbol 1 goes to b. From a and from b both symbols go to c. From c the symbol 0 goes to F and the symbol 1 goes to D. F and D each loop on both symbols. The number of strings of length 6 accepted by this DFA is ____.
variation.explanation: After two symbols the machine is in c whatever they were. The third symbol decides: 0 reaches the absorbing final state F, 1 reaches the absorbing dead state D. So a string is accepted exactly when its third symbol is 0, and the other five symbols are free: $2^5=32$ (a simulation of all 64 strings agrees).

questions.stem: Which of the following regular expressions represent(s) the set of all binary numbers that are divisible by three? Assume that the string $\epsilon$ is divisible by three.

solutionDiagram.alt: Three-state DFA for binary numbers divisible by three. State r is the remainder so far; reading bit b moves r to (2r+b) mod 3. State 0 loops on 0 and moves to 1 on 1; state 1 moves to 2 on 0 and back to 0 on 1; state 2 moves to 1 on 0 and loops on 1. State 0 is the start and only accepting state.

steps.title: A DFA for divisibility by 3
steps.body: Reading a binary number from the left, appending the bit $b$ turns the value $v$ into $2v+b$. So the remainder $r$ modulo 3 moves to $(2r+b) \bmod 3$. With states for remainders 0, 1, 2: from 0, bit 0 stays at 0 and bit 1 goes to 1; from 1, bit 0 goes to 2 and bit 1 goes to 0; from 2, bit 0 goes to 1 and bit 1 stays at 2. The start state and the only final state is 0, and $\epsilon$ stays at 0, which matches the assumption that $\epsilon$ is divisible by three.

steps.title: Loops at state 0 give option (A)
steps.body: A string is accepted when it is a sequence of loops that leave state 0 and return to it. There are two kinds of first-return loop. Read 0 and stay: $0$. Or read 1 to reach state 1; at state 1 the closed walks are 0 to state 2, then any number of 1s on the loop at 2, then 0 back to state 1, which is $01^*0$; and finally read 1 back to state 0. The loops at 0 are therefore $0+1(01^*0)^*1$, and the language is their star, which is option (A). Option (C) is the same set, since the star of $0^*X^*$ with $X=1(01^*0)^*1$ is the star of $0+X$.

steps.title: Option (B) by the other route
steps.body: Rewrite the loops at 0 by a different route. Going 0, 1, 0 (via bits 1,1) is the loop $11$. Going to state 1 then to state 2 (bits 1,0), the walk can then loop at 2 on a 1 or on the two-step trip 2 to 1 to 2 reading $00$, and it returns through 2 to 1 to 0 reading $01$. That loop is $10(1+00)^*01$. With the loop $0$ this gives $(0+11+10(1+00)^*01)^*$, option (B).

steps.title: Option (D) fails
steps.body: Test $1001$, which is nine and divisible by three: the DFA goes 0, 1, 2, 1, 0 and accepts it. Every term of (D) starts with $0$ or with $11$, so no string that starts with $10$ is generated and (D) rejects $1001$. So (D) is wrong and the answer is (A), (B), (C).

shortcut.body: Check $1001$ (nine) first: (D) cannot produce it. For the rest, build the three-state DFA and read the loops at state 0 straight off it; (A) is that expression and (C) is the same with an extra star. (B) is the same DFA read through state 2. About 3 minutes. The quick test only eliminates (D); it does not prove (A), (B), (C).

traps.text: Choosing (D) because it looks like (B) with the closing block changed. Every term of (D) starts with $0$ or $11$, so nothing that starts with $10$ is generated, yet $1001$ (nine) is divisible by three.
Leaving out (B) because it does not look like the expression read off the DFA. It describes the same machine through state 2 and generates the same language.
Leaving out (C) because $0^*$ in front of the star looks like an extra. Star over $0^*X^*$ equals star over $0+X$, so (C) equals (A).
Leaving out (A) because the nested stars look unfamiliar. It is the direct reading of the DFA: the loops $0$ and $1(01^*0)^*1$ at state 0.

recognize.clues: The stem names a numeric property (divisible by three) of binary strings and asks which regular expressions represent it. "Assume the empty string is divisible" fixes the start state as final, so the expressions are loops at that state.
recognize.contrast: Unlike a question about "contains" or "ends with", the property depends on a running remainder, so the DFA has states for remainders, not for pattern prefixes.

check.body: Substitute numbers. $110$ is six and $1111$ is fifteen: both should be generated. $101$ is five and $100$ is four: neither should be. An enumeration of every string up to length 9 against $\text{value} \bmod 3 = 0$ finds the options that never disagree, and the one that rejects $1001$ (nine) disagrees at once.

variation.stem: Which of the following regular expressions represent(s) the set of all binary strings with an even number of 1s? Assume that the empty string is included.
variation.explanation: Build the two-state parity machine: even 1s is the start and final state. A trip that leaves and returns reads either a 0 or a 1, any 0s, then another 1, which gives $(0+10^*1)^*$. The star in option D stops on zeros, and option B puts zeros first. questions.stem: Consider the following language. $L = \{w \in \{0,1\}^* \mid w \text{ ends with the substring } 011\}$. Which one of the following deterministic finite automata accepts $L$?
questions.figure: Four DFAs, each with four states q0 (start), q1, q2, q3 in a row; q3 is the only final state. In every option: q0 on 1 loops to q0; q0 on 0 goes to q1; q1 on 0 loops to q1; q1 on 1 goes to q2; q2 on 0 goes to q1; q2 on 1 goes to q3. The options differ only at q3. (A) q3 on 1 loops to q3; q3 on 0 goes to q1. (B) q3 on 0 and on 1 loops to q3. (C) q3 on 1 goes to q2; q3 on 0 goes to q1. (D) q3 on 1 goes to q0; q3 on 0 goes to q1. The drawing has no state names; q0 to q3 are ours.

diagram.alt: Four DFAs A to D, each four states in a row with the last accepting. They share the arrows 1 loop on q0, 0 from q0 to q1, 0 loop on q1, 1 from q1 to q2, 0 from q2 to q1 and 1 from q2 to q3, and differ only in where q3 goes: A loops on 1, B loops on both symbols, C goes to q2 on 1, D goes to q0 on 1.

solutionDiagram.alt: Option D with states named by the longest suffix of the input that is a prefix of 011: empty, 0, 01, 011. The final state 011 returns to q0 on 1 and to state 0 on 0.

options: (A) from q3, the symbol 1 loops to q3 and the symbol 0 goes to q1
(B) q3 loops to itself on both 0 and 1
(C) from q3, the symbol 1 goes to q2 and the symbol 0 goes to q1
(D) from q3, the symbol 1 goes to q0 and the symbol 0 goes to q1

steps.title: The idea behind a "ends with" automaton
steps.body: To accept exactly the strings that end with the pattern $011$, each state records how much of the pattern the input just read ends with: the longest suffix of the input that is also a prefix of $011$. The prefixes are $\varepsilon$, $0$, $01$ and $011$, so four states are enough. The state for $011$ is final. After each new symbol the new state is the longest such suffix of the longer input.

steps.title: Fill in the transitions
steps.body: State $\varepsilon$ (q0): on 0 the input ends with $0$, so go to q1; on 1 the input ends with $1$, which is not a prefix of $011$, so stay at q0. State $0$ (q1): on 0 the input ends with $00$, whose longest useful suffix is $0$, so stay at q1; on 1 it ends with $01$, go to q2. State $01$ (q2): on 0 it ends with $010$, longest useful suffix $0$, go to q1; on 1 it ends with $011$, go to q3. State $011$ (q3): on 0 it ends with $0110$, longest useful suffix $0$, go to q1; on 1 it ends with $0111$, and no suffix of that is a prefix of $011$, so go to q0.

steps.title: Compare the options
steps.body: All four options already agree on q0, q1 and q2; they differ at q3 on 1. (A) loops at q3 on 1, so it accepts $0111$, which ends with $111$, not $011$. (B) makes q3 a trap that accepts every string that contains $011$ followed by anything, so it accepts $0110$. (C) sends q3 on 1 to q2, which treats $0111$ as if it ended in $01$, so it accepts $01111$: from q2 on 1 reaches q3. (D) sends q3 on 1 to q0, as derived. The answer is (D).

shortcut.body: The four drawings agree except for the arrow from the final state on 1, so look only there. After $0111$ no part of $011$ can be reused, so the machine must restart at q0: option (D). About 40 seconds. Safe because the drawings really share every other arrow.

traps.text: Choosing (A) by thinking the machine can sit in the final state while 1s keep arriving. $0111$ ends with $111$, not $011$, so it must be rejected.
Choosing (B), the automaton for "contains $011$". Once the substring has appeared the final state is never left, so strings like $0110$ are wrongly accepted.
Choosing (C) by treating the last two symbols $11$ as the progress state "$01$". The input $0111$ ends with $11$ but not $01$, so the progress is lost and q0 is correct.

recognize.clues: The language is "ends with the substring 011", and the four drawings share q0, q1, q2 and differ only at the final state. A pattern at the end of the string means states record progress through the pattern.
recognize.contrast: "Contains 011" would make the final state absorbing (option B). "Ends with 011" must let the machine leave the final state, because later symbols can destroy the match.

check.body: Run strings through the chosen DFA. $011$ and $01011$ and $011011$ end in $011$ and reach q3. $0110$ falls to q1, then needs $11$ to return. $0111$ goes q3 then on 1 back to q0, so it is rejected. A comparison of this machine against "ends with 011" for every string to length 9 agrees.

questions.stem: Which one of the following regular expressions represents the set of all binary strings with an odd number of 1's?
questions.keyNote: The official key is MTA, marks to all, because none of the four expressions is correct. (A) generates strings with an even number of 1s such as 1111 and misses 01. (B) always ends in 1, so it misses 10. (C) always starts with 1, so it misses 01. (D) is the closest: it lacks the 0* before the last 1, so it misses every string with one 1 that has a 0 before it, such as 01, 001 and 010. The correct expression is (0*10*10*)*0*10*. We record D as the nearest option. Checked by enumeration of all strings of length up to 8.

steps.title: What the language needs
steps.body: A binary string has an odd number of 1s when, reading from the left, the parity of the 1s seen so far ends as odd. A regular expression for the set must generate every such string, including those with leading zeros or trailing zeros, and nothing else. The building block $0^*10^*10^*$ reads exactly two 1s with any zeros around them, so its star reads an even number of 1s. One more 1, with any zeros around it, makes the count odd.

steps.title: Test the options on short strings
steps.body: The strings $10$ and $01$ each have a single 1, so both belong to the language. (B) always ends with the symbol 1, so it cannot generate $10$. (C) always starts with $1$, so it cannot generate $01$. (A) cannot generate $01$ either, and it also generates $1111$, which has four 1s. (D) is the expression above without the $0^*$ before the final 1, so it cannot generate $01$, $001$ or $010$: any string whose only 1 comes after a 0.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Every option fails at least once, so no option correctly represents the language. The answer key records MTA, which awards the mark to every candidate. The option nearest to the language is (D), which is missing only a $0^*$.

shortcut.body: Try the two strings $01$ and $10$, each with a single 1, so both must be generated. (B) always ends in 1 and fails $10$; (A), (C) and (D) all fail $01$. No option survives, which is why the key is MTA. If you must mark one, (D) is nearest. About 1 minute.

traps.text: Choosing (A) because $(0+1)^*$ looks like the free part before the last 1. The star of $(0+1)^*1(0+1)^*1$ can read $111$ as one round, so with the final $1$ it generates $1111$, which has an even number of 1s.
Choosing (B) because the part before the last 1 is right. The expression must end in 1, so it cannot generate $10$, whose last symbol is 0.
Choosing (C) because it begins with the odd 1 and then adds pairs. It cannot start with 0, so $01$ is lost.
Choosing (D) as the correct expression. It lacks the $0^*$ before the final 1, so it misses $01$; it is only the nearest option, and the institute gave the mark to all.

recognize.clues: The stem asks which regular expression represents "an odd number of 1's" and the four options are built from blocks $0^*10^*10^*$ and a trailing $10^*$ or $0^*1$. The skill is testing short strings against each form.
recognize.contrast: This is a regular-expression writing question, not an automaton one. The two-state parity DFA gives the answer by loops, but the options differ only in where zeros may sit, which small strings expose faster.

check.body: Repair the pattern and test it: $(0^*10^*10^*)^*0^*10^*$ generates $01$, $10$, $0100$ and $11010$ and rejects $11$ and $0$, and an enumeration of all strings up to length 8 shows it matches the odd-parity set exactly. Each given option fails at least one of $01$, $10$ or $1111$, so none equals it.

questions.stem: Consider the following statements. I. If $L_1 \cup L_2$ is regular, then both $L_1$ and $L_2$ must be regular. II. The class of regular languages is closed under infinite union. Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?

steps.title: What closure promises
steps.body: A class of languages is closed under an operation when applying the operation to members of the class always gives a member of the class. Regular languages are closed under union of two languages, hence under any finite union. A closure property says nothing about the reverse direction: knowing that a result is regular does not make its inputs regular. And closure under a finite number of operands does not carry over to infinitely many.

steps.title: Statement I is false
steps.body: Take $L_1=\{a^nb^n \mid n\ge 0\}$, which is not regular, and $L_2=\overline{L_1}$, its complement, which is not regular either because regular languages are closed under complement. Their union is $\{a,b\}^*$, since every string is in $L_1$ or not in it, and that is regular. So a regular union can have non-regular parts.

steps.title: Statement II is false
steps.body: Every single string is a regular language, so each $\{a^nb^n\}$ with one value of $n$ is regular. The union of these languages over all $n\ge 0$ is $\{a^nb^n \mid n \ge 0\}$, which is not regular. So an infinite union of regular languages can be non-regular, and the class is not closed under infinite union. Neither statement is true: (D).

shortcut.body: Both statements have one-line counterexamples with $\{a^nb^n\}$: its complement pairs with it for I, and its strings taken one by one give II. About 1 minute. Safe, since a single counterexample is enough for each.

traps.text: Choosing I by reading closure backwards: a regular union does not force each part to be regular, as $L_1$ and its complement show.
Choosing II by extending finite closure to infinite unions. An infinite union of single-string languages builds $\{a^nb^n\}$.
Choosing both by trusting closure for I and II alike. Each fails for its own reason.

recognize.clues: The stem gives a union whose result is regular and asks about its parts, and also asks about an infinite union. Both are questions about what closure under union does and does not promise.
recognize.contrast: Closure under finite union is true and has a short proof. Do not extend it backwards to the inputs, or outwards to infinitely many operands; the two statements here fail for these two different reasons.

questions.stem: Consider the following language. $L = \{x \in \{a,b\}^* \mid \text{number of } a\text{'s in } x \text{ is divisible by 2 but not divisible by 3}\}$. The minimum number of states in a DFA that accepts $L$ is ____.

solutionDiagram.alt: Six states in a ring numbered 0 to 5, counting the number of a symbols modulo 6; reading a moves one step round the ring and reading b stays. State 0 is the start; states 2 and 4 are accepting.

steps.title: Counting states with Myhill-Nerode
steps.body: The minimum number of states of a DFA equals the number of classes of strings that cannot be told apart: two strings $u$ and $v$ are in the same class when every continuation $z$ gives $uz\in L \iff vz\in L$. Different classes need different states, and one state per class suffices.

steps.title: What a string needs to remember
steps.body: Membership depends only on the number $n$ of $a$s: the $b$s do not matter. The condition "divisible by 2 and not divisible by 3" depends on $n \bmod 2$ and $n \bmod 3$, and by the Chinese remainder theorem the pair is equivalent to $n \bmod 6$. Among $n=0,\dots,5$ the accepted residues are those that are even and not multiples of 3, namely 2 and 4 (0 is a multiple of 3). So a string needs to remember at most $n \bmod 6$, and six states suffice.

steps.title: No two residues can be merged
steps.body: Two strings with residues $i\ne j$ are separated by the continuation $a^m$ whenever exactly one of $i+m$ and $j+m$ lies in $\{2,4\}$ modulo 6. The accepted set $\{2,4\}$ is not unchanged by any non-zero shift: shifting by 1 gives $\{3,5\}$, by 2 gives $\{4,0\}$, by 3 gives $\{5,1\}$, by 4 gives $\{0,2\}$, by 5 gives $\{1,3\}$. So all six residues are pairwise distinguishable and the minimum is 6.

shortcut.body: Two counters, mod 2 and mod 3, combine into one counter mod $\operatorname{lcm}(2,3)=6$. Check that the accepting set $\{2,4\}$ has no smaller period, and the answer is 6. About 1.5 minutes. The method fails when the accepting set repeats with a shorter period, because then states merge.

traps.text: Answering 5 by adding $2+3$. Tracking the two remainders together needs $2\times 3=6$ states, not their sum.
Answering 7 by adding a dead state. No residue is hopeless, since reading more $a$s reaches an accepting residue from every state, so there is no dead state.

recognize.clues: The stem gives no automaton and asks for the minimum number of states for a language defined by counting $a$s with two divisibility conditions, so the count has to come from distinguishable classes of strings.
recognize.contrast: State minimization starts from a given DFA and merges equivalent states. Here no DFA is given, so build the classes of strings directly and show they cannot be merged.

check.body: Check the claim that nothing can be merged on the two accepting residues. With the accepting residues $\{2,4\}$ in a ring of six, the continuation $a^2$ moves residue 2 to residue 4, which accepts, and residue 4 to residue 0, which rejects. So even the two accepting states must stay apart.

questions.stem: If $L$ is a regular language over $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$, which one of the following languages is NOT regular?

steps.title: Closure properties to use
steps.body: Regular languages are closed under reversal, concatenation, and the operations "all prefixes" and "all suffixes". Reversal: reverse every arrow of an automaton and swap the start and final roles. Prefix: in a DFA for $L$, make final every state from which some final state can be reached. Suffix: let the new automaton start from any state that is reachable from the old start state. The question asks for the one operation that can leave the regular languages.

steps.title: A, C and D stay regular
steps.body: (A) $L^R$ is regular by closure under reversal, and $\{xy\mid x\in L, y^R\in L\}$ is $L$ concatenated with $L^R$, which is regular because concatenation preserves regularity. (C) and (D) are the prefix and suffix constructions above, so both are regular.

steps.title: B can be non-regular
steps.body:
Take $L=\{a,b\}^*$, which is regular. Then $\{ww^R\mid w\in L\}$ is the set of even-length palindromes. To accept it, an automaton must remember all of $w$ to compare it with the reversal, which a finite automaton cannot do for unbounded $w$. Take any two different strings $u
e v$ of equal length. Then $uu^R$ is in the language, but $vu^R$ is not, because it is a palindrome only when $v=u$. So $u$ and $v$ lead to different states, and there are infinitely many such strings, which needs infinitely many states. The language is not regular for this $L$, so the answer is (B).
steps.tex: u\cdot u^R\in\{ww^R\},\qquad v\cdot u^R\notin\{ww^R\}\ \text{for } v\ne u,\ |v|=|u|

shortcut.body: Only (B) needs unbounded memory, since it compares $w$ with its mirror image. The other three are standard closure operations on one language, with no coupling between two copies. About 30 seconds. Safe, as the three others are textbook closures.

traps.text: Choosing (A) because $xy$ with $y^R\in L$ looks like a mirror condition. Here $x$ and $y$ are chosen independently, so it is just $L\cdot L^R$, a concatenation.
Choosing (C) because "exists $y$" feels like an unbounded search. In a DFA that search is a reachability check on the finite graph.
Choosing (D) for the same reason as (C): "exists $x$" is handled by letting the automaton start from any reachable state.

questions.stem: For $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$, let us consider the regular language $L=\{x \mid x=a^{2+3k} \text{ or } x=b^{10+12k},\ k\ge 0\}$. Which one of the following can be a pumping length (the constant guaranteed by the pumping lemma) for $L$?

steps.title: What a pumping length is
steps.body: A number $p$ is a pumping length for $L$ if every string $w\in L$ with $|w|\ge p$ can be written $w=xyz$ with $|y|\ge 1$, $|xy|\le p$ and $xy^iz\in L$ for every $i\ge 0$. The condition only concerns strings of length at least $p$. So a number is tested by finding a string of length at least $p$ in $L$ that cannot be pumped, and if there is none, the number works.

steps.title: 3, 5 and 9 fail on the string b^10
steps.body: Take $w=b^{10}\in L$. For $p\le 10$ its length is at least $p$, so it must be pumpable with $y=b^j$ and $1\le j\le |xy|\le p\le 9$. But then $xy^2z=b^{10+j}$ and this lies in $L$ only if $10+j\equiv 10 \pmod{12}$, that is $12\mid j$, which is impossible for $1\le j\le 9$. So $p=3,5,9$ are not pumping lengths.

steps.title: 24 works
steps.body: Let $w\in L$ with $|w|\ge 24$. If $w=a^n$ with $n=2+3k\ge 24$, take $y=aaa$ among the first three symbols: $a^{n+3(i-1)}$ keeps the form $2+3k_2$ and stays long enough, even for $i=0$ since $n-3\ge 2$. If $w=b^n$ with $n=10+12k\ge 24$, then $n\ge 34$; take $y=b^{12}$ among the first twelve symbols: removing or adding blocks of twelve keeps $n\equiv 10 \pmod{12}$ and $n-12\ge 22\ge 10$. In both cases $|xy|\le 12\le 24$. So 24 is a pumping length (any number from 12 up works). The answer is (D).

shortcut.body: The $b$-part forces any pumped block to be a multiple of 12 symbols inside the first $p$ symbols, so a valid $p$ is at least 12 (the strings $b^{10}$ and $b^{22}$ rule out smaller values). Only $24$ qualifies. About 1.5 minutes. The 12 comes from the period of the $b$ part, not from the $a$ part, whose period is only 3.

traps.text: Choosing 3 because the $a$-part pumps with blocks of three. The $b$-part needs blocks of twelve, and $b^{10}$ is longer than 3.
Choosing 5 from $2+3$, the smallest $a$ string plus its period. It ignores the $b$ strings, which fail it just as they fail 3.
Choosing 9 because it is below 10 and seems safe for $b^{10}$. A pumping length must cover the block of twelve, and $b^{10}$ is exactly where 9 fails.

recognize.clues: The stem asks which number can be a pumping length for a regular language, and the language is two arithmetic progressions of lengths, $2+3k$ and $10+12k$. The periods 3 and 12 decide how large the block $y$ must be.
recognize.contrast: The usual pumping question proves a language is not regular by finding a bad string. Here the language is regular and the lemma only promises that some constant exists, so you test the candidate values instead.

questions.stem: Let $\Sigma$ be the set of all bijections from $\{1,\dots,5\}$ to $\{1,\dots,5\}$, where $id$ denotes the identity function, i.e. $id(j)=j,\ \forall j$. Let $\circ$ denote composition on functions. For a string $x=x_1x_2\cdots x_n\in\Sigma^n$, $n\ge 0$, let $\pi(x)=x_1\circ x_2\circ\cdots\circ x_n$. Consider the language $L=\{x\in\Sigma^* \mid \pi(x)=id\}$. The minimum number of states in any DFA accepting $L$ is ____.

steps.title: The alphabet is a group
steps.body: There are $5!=120$ bijections of a 5-element set, so $\Sigma$ has 120 symbols. Composition of bijections is associative, there is an identity, and every bijection has an inverse. The strings over $\Sigma$ multiply into one permutation $\pi(x)$. $L$ is the set of strings whose product is the identity.

steps.title: 120 states are enough
steps.body: After reading a prefix $x$, the only thing that matters for the future is the permutation $g=\pi(x)$, because reading a further symbol $f$ gives $g\circ f$. So a DFA whose states are the 120 permutations, with start $id$, transition $\delta(g,f)=g\circ f$ and the single final state $id$, accepts $L$. It has at most 120 states.

steps.title: No two permutations can share a state
steps.body:
Each permutation $g$ is reached by the one-symbol string $g$. Take two different permutations $g
e h$ and the continuation $g^{-1}$. Then $\pi(g\,g^{-1})=id$, so $g\,g^{-1}\in L$, while $\pi(h\,g^{-1})=h\circ g^{-1}
e id$ because $h
e g$. The two prefixes are told apart, so all 120 prefix classes are different and 120 states are needed. The minimum is 120. There is no dead state, since every state can still reach $id$ by reading an inverse.

shortcut.body: A word problem in a finite group of size $N$ with every group element as a symbol needs exactly $N$ states: one per group element, because the inverse separates any two. Here $N=5!=120$. About 1 minute. Safe, since the alphabet contains every element.

traps.text: Answering 121 by adding a dead state. No state is dead: from any permutation, the inverse symbol brings the product back to the identity.
Answering 24 or 720 by taking the wrong factorial. The bijections are on 5 points, so there are $5!=120$ of them.

recognize.clues: The alphabet is a set of bijections, a string is judged by the composition of its symbols, and acceptance means the product is the identity. The question asks for the minimum DFA size, which is a count of prefix classes.
recognize.contrast: A counting language such as divisibility by $m$ has one state per remainder. This is the same idea with group elements in place of remainders, and the inverse symbol plays the role that adding the rest of the count plays there.

check.body: Test the pattern on the smallest case. The bijections of $\{1,2\}$ are the identity and the swap, and the language is the strings with an even number of swaps. Its minimal DFA has 2 states, which equals $2!$, matching the count of group elements.

questions.stem: Let $N$ be an NFA with $n$ states. Let $k$ be the number of states of a minimal DFA which is equivalent to $N$. Which one of the following is necessarily true?

steps.title: Terms, and the rule that decides the question
steps.body: A DFA (deterministic finite automaton) has exactly one arrow for each state and symbol. An NFA (nondeterministic finite automaton) may have several arrows, or none, for a state and symbol; it accepts a string if at least one path ends in an accepting state. Two automata are equivalent when they accept the same language. The minimal DFA of a language is the DFA with the fewest states that accepts it. Here $n$ is the number of NFA states and $k$ is the size of that minimal DFA. "Necessarily true" means true for every NFA, so one NFA that breaks a statement kills it. The deciding rule is the subset construction: build a DFA whose states are sets of NFA states, where the set reached after reading a string is every NFA state that some path for that string can reach.

steps.title: An upper bound: at most 2^n sets
steps.body: An NFA with $n$ states has exactly $2^n$ subsets of states, counting the empty set. Every DFA state of the subset construction is one of these subsets, so the construction gives an equivalent DFA with at most $2^n$ states. The minimal DFA is never larger than any equivalent DFA, so for every NFA

steps.title: A and B fail: the minimal DFA can be tiny
steps.body: Take the NFA with $n=3$ states in which every state loops on both symbols and the start state is accepting. It accepts every string over $\{a,b\}$. The minimal DFA for "all strings" is a single accepting state with a self-loop, so $k=1$. Then $k\ge 2^n=8$ is false and $k\ge n=3$ is false, so neither (A) nor (B) is necessary.

steps.title: C fails: the blow-up can pass n^2
steps.body: Take the language "the 6th symbol from the right end is $a$". An NFA guesses the position: the start state loops on both symbols, reads $a$ into a chain of 6 further states, and the last state accepts. That is $n=7$ states. A DFA must remember the last 6 symbols, because two different 6-symbol windows can be told apart by some suffix that moves the deciding position onto the place where they differ. That needs $2^6=64$ states, and a script that runs the subset construction and minimises confirms $k=64$. Since $64>7^2=49$, the statement $k\le n^2$ is not necessary. Only (D) holds for every NFA, so the answer is (D).

shortcut.body: Recall the subset construction: an $n$-state NFA gives a DFA with at most $2^n$ states, so (D) is the textbook upper bound. Kill (A) and (B) with the NFA for "all strings", whose minimal DFA has one state. About 40 seconds. Safe: the three wrong options are all refuted by one tiny NFA each.

traps.text: Choosing (A) because $2^n$ is the famous number. It is the worst case, reached only by special NFAs such as "the $(n-1)$th symbol from the end is $a$". The all-strings NFA with 3 states has a 1-state minimal DFA.

Choosing (B) on the feeling that a deterministic machine needs at least as many states as the nondeterministic one. Nondeterminism can waste states: three NFA states for "all strings" collapse to one DFA state.

Choosing (C) because $n^2$ is the size of a product construction. The subset construction is exponential, not quadratic: the 7-state NFA for "6th symbol from the end is $a$" needs 64 DFA states, which exceeds $49$.

recognize.clues: The stem relates $n$, the states of an NFA, to $k$, the states of its minimal DFA, and asks what is necessarily true. That is a question about the size change in the NFA to DFA conversion.
recognize.contrast: Minimization only shrinks a given DFA, while the subset construction can grow it. The construction gives an upper bound on $k$; it never gives a lower bound, because a redundant NFA can collapse to a tiny DFA.

check.body: Test the boundary $n=1$. A one-state NFA has only 2 subsets of states, so $k\le 2^1=2$. The value 2 is reached: over $\{a,b\}$ the one-state accepting NFA that loops only on $a$ accepts $a^*$, and its minimal complete DFA needs a dead state for $b$. A three-state NFA for all strings gives $k=1$, below $n$, so no lower bound in terms of $n$ can hold.

The order of a language $L$ is defined as the smallest $k$ such that $L^k=L^{k+1}$. Consider the language $L_1$ (over alphabet $0$) accepted by the following automaton. The order of $L_1$ is ______.
questions.figure: A three-state automaton over the single symbol 0. The start state q0 is accepting; q0 on 0 goes to q1, which is also accepting. q1 on 0 goes to q2, which is not accepting, and q2 on 0 goes back to q1. The drawing has no state names; q0, q1, q2 are ours.

solutionDiagram.alt: Rows of boxes for the lengths in L^0, L^1, L^2 and L^3. L^1 holds 0 and the odd lengths, while L^2 and L^3 both hold every length, so the order is 2.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: A language is a set of strings. The concatenation $A\cdot B$ is the set of all strings $xy$ with $x\in A$ and $y\in B$. So $L^i$ is the set of strings made by gluing $i$ strings of $L$ together, and $L^0=\{\epsilon\}$ is gluing none. The order is the first power $k$ at which $L^k$ and $L^{k+1}$ are the same set. Every string here is a run of zeros, $0^n$, and gluing $0^a$ to $0^b$ gives $0^{a+b}$. So we can describe each language by the set of lengths $n$ it contains, and concatenation becomes adding lengths.

steps.title: What L1 contains
steps.body: An automaton accepts a string if reading it ends in an accepting state. The start state q0 accepts, so $\epsilon\in L_1$ (length 0). One $0$ leads to q1, which accepts (length 1). A second $0$ leads to q2, which does not accept. A third $0$ returns to q1, which accepts, and the automaton alternates q1, q2, q1, ... So length $n\ge1$ is accepted exactly when $n$ is odd. steps.title: The first powers, one at a time
steps.body: $L^0=\{\epsilon\}$ has the single length 0, and $L^1=L$ has many, so $L^0\neq L^1$. For $L^2=L\cdot L$ add any two lengths from $L$. Adding 0 to any length of $L$ gives 0 and all odd lengths. Adding two odd lengths gives every even length from 2 up, because $2m=1+(2m-1)$. So $L^2$ holds every length: $L^2=0^*$. In particular length 2 is in $L^2$ but not in $L^1$, so $L^1\neq L^2$.

steps.title: Where the powers stop changing
steps.body: $L^3=L^2\cdot L=0^*\cdot L$. It cannot contain anything outside $0^*$, and it contains all of $0^*$ because $\epsilon\in L$ lets us glue the empty string on. So $L^3=0^*=L^2$. The first equal neighbours are $L^2$ and $L^3$, so the smallest $k$ with $L^k=L^{k+1}$ is $k=2$, which matches the official key.
steps.tex: L^0\neq L^1,\quad L^1\neq L^2,\quad L^2=L^3\ \Rightarrow\ k=2

shortcut.body: Read $L$ as lengths $\{0,1,3,5,\dots\}$. Since $1\in L$ and $1+1=2$, $1+3=4$, and so on, two odd lengths already give every even length, so $L^2$ is all lengths and $L^3$ cannot add anything. $L^1$ misses 2, so the answer is 2. About 1.5 minutes. Safe here because the alphabet has one symbol and $\epsilon\in L$, so powers only grow.

traps.text: Answering 1 because $L$ looks closed under gluing. It is not: $0\cdot 0=00$ has length 2, which is even, and $L$ has no even length above 0. So $L^2$ is strictly bigger than $L$.
Answering 3 by stopping one step late. You find $L^2=L^3$ and report the index of the second set. The definition asks for the smaller index $k$ of the equal pair $L^k=L^{k+1}$.

Answering 0 because $L^0=\{\epsilon\}$ looks like the starting point that already repeats. It does not: $L^1=L$ also holds the odd lengths, so $L^0\neq L^1$. Counting the automaton's 3 states is a different slip, because the order is about powers of the language, not about states.

recognize.clues: The stem defines $L^i$ by repeated concatenation and an order by when the powers stop changing, over an alphabet with the single symbol 0. Over one symbol, concatenation is addition of lengths.
recognize.contrast: The Kleene star $L^*$ is the union of all powers. The order asks where the powers themselves first stop changing, and that can happen long before the union is taken.

check.body: Check that length 2 is the witness. The automaton never accepts length 2, because the second state is not accepting, so $0^2\notin L^1$. But $0^2=0\cdot 0$ with both factors of length 1 in $L$, so $0^2\in L^2$. Hence $L^1\ne L^2$, and no earlier index can be the order either.

The accepting states are $q_0$ and $q_1$. The order of $L$ is ____.

Adding three gives every length, so $L^3$ is all of $0^*$, and $L^4$ is the same. A script that computes the powers confirms $L^2\ne L^3=L^4$, so the order is 3.

questions.stem: Let $\delta$ denote the transition function and $\hat{\delta}$ denote the extended transition function of the $\epsilon$-NFA whose transition table is given below. Then $\hat{\delta}(q_2, aba)$ is

solutionDiagram.alt: The epsilon-NFA with dashed epsilon arrows between q0 and q2 and from q1 to q2, and the trace of reading a, b, a from q2: {q0,q2}, then {q0,q1,q2}, then {q0,q2,q3}, then {q0,q1,q2}.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: An $\epsilon$-NFA is an NFA that may also change state on an $\epsilon$-move, an arrow that reads no input symbol. The $\epsilon$-closure of a state $p$ is the set of all states reachable from $p$ by following only $\epsilon$ arrows (including $p$ itself). The extended function $\hat{\delta}(p,w)$ is the set of states the machine can be in after reading the whole string $w$ starting from $p$, with $\epsilon$ moves allowed anywhere. It is built by two rules: $\hat{\delta}(p,\epsilon)$ is the closure of $p$, and for each further symbol, move every state in the current set along that symbol, then close the result under $\epsilon$ moves.

steps.title: Closures of the four states
steps.body: Follow the $\epsilon$ column. From $q_0$ we reach $q_2$, and from $q_2$ we reach $q_0$ again, so closure($q_0$) = $\{q_0,q_2\}$. From $q_2$ the same two states, so closure($q_2$) = $\{q_0,q_2\}$. From $q_1$ we reach $q_2$ and then $q_0$, so closure($q_1$) = $\{q_0,q_1,q_2\}$. State $q_3$ has no $\epsilon$ arrow, so closure($q_3$) = $\{q_3\}$.

steps.title: Start and read the first a
steps.body: Before any symbol, the machine started in $q_2$ can already be in closure($q_2$) = $\{q_0,q_2\}$. Now read $a$: $q_0$ goes to $q_1$, and $q_2$ has no $a$ arrow, so it dies. The moved set is $\{q_1\}$. Close it: closure($q_1$) = $\{q_0,q_1,q_2\}$.

steps.title: Read b
steps.body: Move each state of $\{q_0,q_1,q_2\}$ on $b$: $q_0\to q_0$, $q_1\to q_3$, $q_2\to\emptyset$. The moved set is $\{q_0,q_3\}$. Close it: closure($q_0$) adds $q_2$, and closure($q_3$) adds nothing. This gives $\{q_0,q_2,q_3\}$.

steps.title: Read the last a and match the option
steps.body: Move each state of $\{q_0,q_2,q_3\}$ on $a$: $q_0\to q_1$, while $q_2$ and $q_3$ have no $a$ arrow. The moved set is $\{q_1\}$ and its closure is $\{q_0,q_1,q_2\}$. This is option (C), matching the official key.

shortcut.body: Keep one set in your head and repeat two moves per symbol: move on the symbol, then add every state reachable by $\epsilon$. Start with $\{q_0,q_2\}$ and the sets are $\{q_0,q_1,q_2\}$, $\{q_0,q_2,q_3\}$, $\{q_0,q_1,q_2\}$. About 2 minutes. Never skip the closure at the start: that is where most errors begin.

traps.text: Choosing (A) because $q_2$ has no $a$ arrow in the table, so the string seems to die at once. The machine may first take $\epsilon$ from $q_2$ to $q_0$, and $q_0$ does read $a$.

Choosing (B) by mixing states from different steps: the $q_1$ made by the first $a$ with the $q_0$ and $q_3$ made by $b$, and forgetting to close under $\epsilon$, which would have added $q_2$ after each step.
Choosing (D), which is the correct set after reading only $ab$. It stops one symbol early; the final $a$ moves the set to $\{q_1\}$ and its closure.

recognize.clues: The stem gives a transition table with an $\epsilon$ column and asks for the extended transition function on the string $aba$ from a named state, so the set must be closed under $\epsilon$ at the start and after each symbol.
recognize.contrast: In a plain NFA the extended function needs no closures. The subset construction uses these same moves to build a whole DFA, but here only one run from one state is needed.

check.body: Confirm each state of the result by a direct path. From $q_2$: $\epsilon$ to $q_0$, read $a$ to $q_1$, $\epsilon$ to $q_2$ and $q_0$, read $b$ to $q_0$, read $a$ to $q_1$. Then $\epsilon$ moves from $q_1$ reach $q_2$ and $q_0$. State $q_3$ cannot appear because its only incoming arrow reads $b$, and the string ends with $a$.

questions.stem: The minimum possible number of states of a deterministic finite automaton that accepts the regular language $L=\{w_1aw_2 \mid w_1,w_2\in\{a,b\}^*,\ |w_1|=2,\ |w_2|\ge 3\}$ is ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: A chain of seven states s0 to s6 where every arrow reads a or b except the arrow out of s2, which must read a; reading b at s2 goes to a dead state D. State s6 accepts and loops.

steps.title: What the language says, and the rule for counting states
steps.body: The notation $|w|$ is the length of $w$. A string is in $L$ if it can be written as $w_1\,a\,w_2$ where $w_1$ is any two symbols, then comes one $a$, then $w_2$ is any three or more symbols. $w_1$ fills positions 1 and 2, so the middle $a$ is always position 3. So $L$ is exactly: strings of length at least 6 whose 3rd symbol is $a$. To find the fewest states of a DFA we use the Myhill-Nerode idea: two prefixes $u$ and $v$ are equivalent if every continuation $z$ gives the same verdict on $uz$ and $vz$ (both in $L$ or both not). A DFA needs at least one state per equivalence class, and a DFA with that many states exists.

steps.title: Sort the prefixes by what they still need
steps.body: A prefix that is already doomed (3rd symbol is $b$) is dead: no continuation ever reaches $L$. Every other prefix is characterised by how many more symbols are needed. The empty prefix needs 6 more at least, a prefix of length 1 needs 5, length 2 needs 4. A prefix of length 3 with 3rd symbol $a$ needs 3 more, length 4 needs 2, length 5 needs 1, and any such prefix of length 6 or more is already in $L$ and needs 0. Prefixes of the same length with a good 3rd symbol behave identically, because the first two symbols are free.

steps.title: The eight classes are all different
steps.body: The list above has eight values: 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0 and none. Two prefixes with different values are distinguished by the shortest continuation of one of them, which the other rejects. So there are at least 8 classes. A script that groups all prefixes up to length 9 by their behaviour on every suffix up to length 8 finds exactly 8 groups.

steps.title: A DFA with 8 states exists
steps.body: Chain $s_0\to s_1\to s_2$ on either symbol. From $s_2$ go to $s_3$ on $a$ and to the dead state $D$ on $b$. Continue $s_3\to s_4\to s_5\to s_6$ on either symbol, with $s_6$ accepting and looping on both symbols, and $D$ looping on both. That is $s_0,\dots,s_6$ and $D$: 8 states. A script checks that it accepts exactly $L$ on every string of length up to 12. The minimum is 8, matching the official key.

shortcut.body: Rewrite the language as: length at least 6 and 3rd symbol $a$. Then count one state per length 0 to 5, plus one accepting state for length 6 or more, plus one dead state for a wrong 3rd symbol: $6+1+1=8$. About 1 minute. The count is safe here because the length-3, 4, 5 states already hold the good third symbol, so no state is added for it.

traps.text: Answering 7 by leaving out the dead state. A DFA needs an arrow for every symbol, and a 3rd symbol $b$ has to go somewhere that never accepts.
Answering 6 by counting only the six positions $|w_1|+1+|w_2|_{\min}$ of the shortest string, with no accepting state that loops and no dead state.
Answering 9 or more by giving each of the four strings of length 2 its own state. The first two symbols are completely free, so all four strings of length 2 are one class.

recognize.clues: The question asks for the minimum number of DFA states of a language built from fixed-length blocks around a single forced symbol, so counting prefix classes is the method.
recognize.contrast: Designing a DFA by hand only gives an upper bound. Myhill-Nerode also proves no smaller DFA exists, which is what a minimum question needs.

check.body: Test the 8-state machine on short strings. The string $bbabbb$ has third symbol $a$ and length 6, so it ends in the looping accepting state. The string $aabbbb$ has third symbol $b$, so it falls into the dead state and is rejected. These two strings only exercise the machine; the lower bound comes from separation. A prefix that still needs $j$ symbols accepts any continuation of length $j$, while a prefix that needs more than $j$ rejects it, so the prefixes needing 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 more symbols are pairwise separated. The accepting state accepts the empty continuation and the dead state rejects every continuation, so they are separated from all the others.

questions.stem: Consider the language $L$ given by the regular expression $(a+b)^*b(a+b)$ over the alphabet $\{a,b\}$. The smallest number of states needed in a deterministic finite-state automaton (DFA) accepting $L$ is ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: A four-state DFA with states aa, ab, ba and bb named for the last two symbols read; ba and bb are accepting. Arrows follow the rule: reading c from state xy goes to state yc.

steps.title: What the expression means, and the rule for counting states
steps.body: In a regular expression, $+$ means "or", so $(a+b)$ is one symbol, either $a$ or $b$, and $^*$ means zero or more repeats. So $(a+b)^*b(a+b)$ is: anything, then a $b$, then exactly one more symbol. A string is in $L$ exactly when its length is at least 2 and its second-last symbol is $b$. To count the fewest DFA states we use the Myhill-Nerode idea: two prefixes $u$ and $v$ are equivalent if every continuation $z$ gives the same verdict on $uz$ and $vz$. A DFA needs one state per equivalence class and no more.

steps.title: What a prefix must remember
steps.body: After reading a prefix, the future verdict depends on the next symbols and on the last two symbols so far: the next symbol will turn the last symbol into the second-last. So a prefix is described by its last two symbols (a missing symbol counts as $a$, since it is not a $b$). That gives at most four classes: $aa$, $ab$, $ba$, $bb$.

steps.title: The four classes are all different
steps.body: The empty continuation separates the accepting classes (second-last symbol $b$: $ba$ and $bb$) from the rejecting ones ($aa$ and $ab$). Inside each pair, continue with the single symbol $a$. From $aa$ it gives $\dots aa\,a$, second-last $a$, rejected; from $ab$ it gives $\dots ab\,a$, second-last $b$, accepted. From $ba$ it gives second-last $a$, rejected; from $bb$ it gives second-last $b$, accepted. So no two classes merge: at least 4 states.

steps.title: Four are enough
steps.body: Reading $c$ in state $xy$ moves to $yc$, with accepting states $ba$ and $bb$ and start state $aa$. A script checks this 4-state DFA against the expression on all strings up to length 12, and a second script groups prefixes by behaviour and finds 4 classes. The answer is 4, matching the official key.

shortcut.body: Translate to "second-last symbol is $b$". A DFA must remember the last two symbols and there are $2^2=4$ combinations, all distinguishable. About 40 seconds. The same reasoning gives $2^n$ for "$n$th symbol from the end", which is why this pattern is a favourite.

traps.text: Answering 3 by counting the states of the obvious NFA: loop on the start state, a $b$ move, and one more move to an accepting state. A DFA cannot guess where the $b$ is, so it needs more.
Answering 8 by applying the full $2^n$ blow-up of the subset construction to that 3-state NFA. Only 4 of the 8 subsets can be reached, and all 4 are distinct.
Answering 5 by adding a dead state. There is none: from every state both symbols lead to a state that can still accept.

recognize.clues: The expression ends in a fixed-length tail after an unrestricted star, so acceptance depends on a symbol at a fixed distance from the end of the input.
recognize.contrast: The three-state NFA for the same expression is smaller. An NFA may guess where the tail starts, while a DFA must remember the window, so the NFA state count does not answer a DFA question.

check.body: Run the four-state machine on $bab$: the last two symbols are $ab$, which is rejecting, as the second-last symbol is $a$. Run it on $abb$: the last two are $bb$, which is accepting. Any machine with only 3 states would send two of the four windows to one state, and the continuation $a$ separates $aa$ from $ab$ and $ba$ from $bb$.
